unresolved.description: KXMLBHR text counts home runs 'in' the game originally scheduled for a date but does not say whether extra-inning home runs count, how a postponed or suspended game settles, or what happens in a rain-shortened official game where the hitter loses PAs.
unresolved.what_would_resolve: Full KXMLBHR rule document and settled examples of an extra-inning home run and a postponed game.

contract.settlement_definition: Two live series with sampled rules: KXMLBRBI (Yes if the named batter records at least N RBIs, e.g. 2+) and KXMLBSB (Yes if he records at least N stolen bases, 1+ sampled). Both use the same gate: the batter must be in the official starting lineup and record at least one plate appearance; a scratch, bench start, zero-PA starter or later-entering substitute settles at the undefined fair market price, and pinch-hit at-bats do not count. The texts say only 'based on RBIs recorded' / 'based on stolen bases recorded'; official-scoring conventions (no RBI on a GIDP, RBI on bases-loaded walk/HBP, no SB on defensive indifference) are presumed. Runs scored have no series: the Kalshi series endpoint (category Sports, read 2026-11-08) lists 166 KXMLB series and none settles on a batter's runs scored (runs appear only inside KXMLBHRR, filed in hitter_hits_and_total_bases). Settled KXMLBRBI markets listed on the same date carry 1+, 2+ and occasionally 3+ rungs; KXMLBSB carries only 1+. Postponement and the data source are not stated.

rules_evidence.quote: If Sal Frelick is in the starting lineup and records at least one plate appearance the market will settle based on RBIs recorded.
rules_evidence.establishes: RBI ladder settles on official RBIs once the starter has at least one PA.

rules_evidence.quote: If Sal Frelick is scratched or not included in the starting lineup, the market will resolve to the fair market price.
rules_evidence.establishes: Scratch or bench status settles at the fair market price rather than resolving No, so the priced population is conditional on starting.

rules_evidence.quote: If Sal Frelick records 2+ RBIs in Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay professional baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 28, 2026
rules_evidence.establishes: Rungs are N+ thresholds on a discrete count with strong zero and one mass.

rules_evidence.quote: If Sal Frelick is in the starting lineup and records at least one plate appearance the market will settle based on stolen bases recorded.
rules_evidence.establishes: The stolen-base ladder, now filed here, uses the same start-plus-one-PA gate as RBIs, so a starter who is removed before reaching base still settles (usually No).

variants_and_edge_cases: Two live series are filed here (KXMLBRBI and KXMLBSB); runs scored is not traded, so the 'runs' part of the archetype has no contract evidence. A stolen base credited on a delayed or double steal counts; defensive indifference is scored as no SB by convention (presumed).

Official-scoring ASSUMPTION (the Kalshi text only says 'RBIs recorded'): no RBI on a ground-ball double play; an RBI is credited for a run forced in by a bases-loaded walk, hit-by-pitch or catcher interference/obstruction, and for sacrifice flies; an RBI on an error depends on the scorer's judgement that the run would have scored anyway.

Extra innings: in the regular season the automatic runner on second creates extra RBI chances for the hitters due up in the 10th; the sampled contracts are October postseason games, where MLB does not use the automatic runner, so this effect applies only to regular-season variants.
Postponement and suspended-game handling are not stated in the sampled text.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official box score RBIs from MLB Stats API or Retrosheet; presumed since the sampled rules do not name a source.

mechanism.summary: RBIs and stolen bases are both opportunity-conditional counts. An RBI requires runners on base when the hitter bats and an outcome that brings them home under official scoring, so the expected RBIs are a sum over his PAs of the probability of each base-out state times the probability his outcome scores each runner. The base-out state distribution is determined by the hitters ahead (their on-base rates), team scoring and the opposing pitcher, so it is a Markov chain over the lineup. Conversion depends on power, contact and situational outcomes (sacrifice flies, ground balls scoring from third) and excludes double plays. Stolen bases require reaching first (or second), a steal opportunity with the next base open, a decision to go made by runner, manager and game state, and success against the pitcher's time to plate and the catcher's throw. Both outcomes are rare-event counts with zero mass, heavily dependent on lineup slot and the confirmed lineup, and the count distribution is zero-inflated and overdispersed.

stages.name: Lineup gate and neighbours
stages.description: The market settles non-starters at the fair market price; what matters for the surviving population is the batting slot, who bats ahead (supplying runners) and behind (affecting whether pitchers pitch around him and the stolen-base decision). The lineup card posts late, so ahead-of-him on-base skill is not known until then.
stages.distribution: Binary start gate; neighbour identities change the opportunity distribution materially (a leadoff hitter with a .380 OBP ahead versus a .300 OBP).

stages.name: Runner-on-base opportunity chain
stages.description: Opportunity is the distribution of runners on base when the hitter comes to bat in each of his PAs. It is a Markov chain on the order: the on-base rate of preceding batters, the opposing pitcher's baserunner allowance, and the park run environment determine how often a runner stands on first, second or third (and how many outs), and so how often an RBI is possible at all.
stages.distribution: Discrete base-out state distribution per PA; positive dependence among hitters' states within a game; 40-50% of PAs have no runner on base.

stages.name: RBI conversion given runners
stages.description: Conversion depends on the hitter: power and extra-base rate drive scoring multiple runners, contact and ability to hit fly balls with a runner on third (sacrifice flies), ground-ball tendencies (double plays do not give RBIs) and walk behaviour with the bases loaded. Conversion differs by runner position: a runner on third scores on many outs, a runner on first on few.
stages.distribution: Per-opportunity Bernoulli-like with heavy tail from HR with traffic; correlated with team scoring.

stages.name: Stolen-base attempt and success
stages.description: Stealing needs the hitter on first (or second) with the next base open, then an attempt decision: runner speed and success history, the pitcher's time to the plate and left-handed pickoff, the catcher's pop time and arm, score margin and inning, the manager's green light, and rule changes (bigger bases, pickoff limits) that moved attempt rates. Success then depends on the same battery.
stages.distribution: Rare Bernoulli per opportunity (attempt about 5-10% of first-base opportunities for typical runners, higher for elite); multiple SBs per game possible but rare.

stages.name: Count distribution and ladder nesting
stages.description: RBI and SB counts are zero-inflated and overdispersed relative to a simple Poisson because opportunities cluster in high-scoring innings and one event (a grand slam) can add four; the thresholds 1+ and 2+ for RBI and 1+ for SB are nested events from the same latent opportunity.
stages.distribution: Zero-inflated, right-skewed; RBI heavy tail with clustered runs; SB nearly Bernoulli with small multiple mass.

availability_news.note: Scratch settles at fair market price; card posting.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest and clinched-seed behaviour change RBI and SB totals only by changing who starts and where he bats; no separate schedule driver exists beyond the lineup card, and no stakes effect on a batter's RBI conversion is documented.

officiating_rules.note: RBI scoring rules (no RBI on a GIDP or error) are definitional and covered under settlement; umpire zone has no first-order effect on RBI or SB counts and the 2023 pickoff-limit and base-size rules are handled as the rule regime input.

mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.label: Per-PA base-out state distribution from the confirmed lineup (Markov chain)
mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.mechanism: RBI opportunity is the probability distribution of runners and outs when the hitter bats, derived from the hitters ahead.
mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.rationale: Average RBI opportunity per slot hides lineup-specific variation: the same cleanup hitter has materially more RBI chances behind two .380-OBP hitters than behind two .300-OBP hitters, and opposing starter baserunner allowance scales it.
mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.measurement: Markov chain over 24 transient base-out states (8 base occupancy sets x 0/1/2 outs) plus the inning-end absorbing state, with per-batter outcome probabilities (1B, 2B, 3B, HR, BB/HBP, K, GIDP, other out, reach on error) from batter rates shrunk to league with k = 200 PA, log5-adjusted to the starter (first 2.5 times through) then bullpen, with park multiplier. Runner advancement probabilities from league event data by outcome and base-out state. Solve analytically across the 9-slot order for 9 innings; for each batter's n-th PA output the distribution of (runners on base, outs) and the expected runners on base per PA. Units: expected runners per PA. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: confirmed lineup and batter hand splits
mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain.why: Exact RBI-opportunity input for the lineup and opponent; avoids averaging slot opportunity over lineups.

mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.label: RBI conversion rate by runner position (1B/2B/3B) and outs, excluding GIDP
mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.mechanism: Given runners, the hitter's chance to drive them in differs by base and outs and includes sacrifice flies, productive outs and HR.
mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.rationale: A batter's RBI per runner on base differs for a power hitter (HR clears everyone) versus a contact hitter (scores runner from third on a fly ball) versus a ground-ball hitter (GIDP, no RBI). Aggregated RBI/PA mixes these roles with opportunity.
mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.measurement: For each hitter over 3 seasons (half-life 600 PA): RBI per PA in each of the 7 non-empty base states (1B, 2B, 3B, 1B2B, 1B3B, 2B3B, loaded) x 3 outs, from event data, with RBI credited per official scoring (excluding runs on error/GIDP per rule). Shrink each cell to the hitter's hand-class cell with k = 40 PA in that cell, and each hand-class cell to league with k = 200 PA. Components reported: P(HR), P(hit), P(sac fly | 3B, <2 outs), P(GIDP | 1B, <2 outs). Combine with the lineup's base-out distribution from mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain to get expected RBI per PA. Units: RBI per PA given state. As-of: through the prior game.
raw_data: PA-level: base-out state, outcome, RBI credited, batter, pitcher
mlb.rbi_conversion_by_runner_base.why: Separates opportunity from conversion so the model knows why a hitter has RBIs; avoids regressing noisy RISP batting average.

mlb.sb_opportunity_conversion.label: Steal attempt hazard per opportunity (runner on first, second base open) by game state
mlb.sb_opportunity_conversion.mechanism: A steal attempt is a decision at each opportunity influenced by runner, battery, score and rule regime.
mlb.sb_opportunity_conversion.rationale: Season SB totals mix opportunity (how often the runner reaches first) with decision and success; the contract is per game so opportunity is the pivotal driver, and the decision probability depends on score margin (late blowouts suppress steals), pitcher hand and the pickoff-disengagement rule.
mlb.sb_opportunity_conversion.measurement: For each runner over 2 seasons (2023+ rule regime only): attempts / opportunities where opportunity = PA-end or between-PA state with runner on first and second open and fewer than two outs; stratify by pitcher hand (L/R), score margin (|margin|<=3 vs >3) and inning (<=6, >=7). Shrink to speed-class rate with k = 30 opportunities. Multiply by P(opportunity) = P(reach first) from lineup chain and by success probability (runner success rate vs battery pop time + time to plate, shrunk k = 25 attempts). Units: steals per game. As-of: lineup post (catcher and pitcher known).
free_sources: Baseball Savant running splits and sprint speed
Statcast pop time and pitcher time to plate
raw_data: opportunity-level: runner, pitcher, catcher, score, inning, attempt, success
mlb.sb_opportunity_conversion.why: Provides an exact per-game decomposition for the 1+ steals ladder instead of season SB rate times PA.

mlb.batting_behind_protection.label: Quality of the hitters batting behind (on-deck and following) as a pitch-around and intentional-walk driver
mlb.batting_behind_protection.mechanism: Pitchers and managers decide whether to pitch to or around a hitter, and whether to hold or send a runner, based on who follows; a weak hitter on deck raises walks and intentional walks for the current hitter and lowers his RBI chances.
mlb.batting_behind_protection.rationale: RBI conversion and steal attempts both depend on the batter behind: with first base open a dangerous on-deck hitter lowers the walk rate, while a weak one invites intentional walks that remove RBI chances. This is stated only in interactions today and has no measurable input; it also changes the green light for a runner on first.
mlb.batting_behind_protection.measurement: For hitter h in slot s of the confirmed lineup, compute protection = mean projected wOBA (vs the starter's hand, shrunk to ZiPS/Steamer with k = 300 PA) of the next two hitters in the order, minus the league mean wOBA, in wOBA points. Convert to expected intentional-plus-unintentional walk-rate shift using a regression of BB% on protection with first-base-open flag over 2021-2025 (shrunk by hitter with k = 200 PA). Output: change in per-PA walk probability and in the P(runner goes) at first base. As-of: lineup post.
free_sources: Retrosheet event files (first-base-open flag, intentional walks)
raw_data: PA events with base-out state and IBB flag
mlb.batting_behind_protection.why: Gives the batting-behind effect on RBI opportunity and stolen-base decisions a measured input instead of leaving it only in an interaction.

mlb.rbi_opportunity.reason: Core RBI driver, but defined as an average; replaced in practice by pa_base_out_state_chain for the confirmed lineup.

mlb.expected_pa.reason: Slot PA count scales opportunities; needs link to team scoring and removal risk. Catalog measurement conditions PA on a market-implied team total; condition on projected team runs from the run model instead, keeping market totals as a BENCHMARK_ONLY comparison.

mlb.lineup_pit.reason: Neighbours and slot determine opportunity; vintage matters.

mlb.hitter_quality.reason: Power and contact skill convert runners, but generic xwOBA mixes OBP (opportunity for others) with conversion.

mlb.team_wrc_vs_hand.reason: Team offence baseline for runner volume; a proxy replaced by the lineup chain.

mlb.sp_quality.reason: Starter run prevention sets baserunner volume; weak per-start predictor for a single hitter.

mlb.bullpen_talent.reason: Late PAs against relievers; low weight for RBI count.

mlb.park.reason: Run environment scales runner volume; modest.

mlb.sb_context.reason: Pitcher hold time and catcher pop time are real determinants of attempt and success; vintage and lineup catcher needed.

mlb.baserunning.reason: Runner attempt/success history overlaps sb_context's attempt-rate component and hitter_speed; keep as the runner-side success term.

mlb.hitter_speed.reason: Sprint speed predicts attempts and success but is correlated with baserunning; its weight is conditional on manager green light.

mlb.rule_regime.reason: Post-2023 rule changes shifted SB baselines; use to restrict training to the current regime.

mlb.team_style.reason: Manager aggressiveness is the unobserved decision variable; measured by team SB attempt rate per opportunity.

mlb.run_scoring_opportunity.reason: Runs-scored opportunity belongs to the runs component of H+R+RBI (a different archetype); no contract in this archetype pays on runs. Verified 2026-11-08: no runs-scored series exists among the 166 KXMLB series, so the archetype's scope is RBI and stolen bases only.

mlb.contact_dist.reason: Count distributions given PA and slot ignore base-out state, which is the dominant driver of RBI; zero inflation is not captured.

m.rules_text.reason: Start-plus-one-PA gate, pinch-hit exclusion and 'RBIs recorded' / 'stolen bases recorded' wording define the settled population for both series now filed here.

m.ladder_structure.reason: Cross-rung price consistency is market-derived; no information about hitters.

interactions.mechanism: RBIs are runners on base times conversion given runners, so a hitter with elite conversion but poor lineup context and a hitter with ordinary conversion in an on-base-heavy lineup can have similar expected RBIs. The product, not a sum, is the right structure, and zero-runner PAs contribute no RBI except a solo home run.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare a model with opportunity x conversion terms versus additive terms on RBI count calibration.

interactions.mechanism: Steal probability is opportunity times attempt hazard times success; slow pitchers and weak-armed catchers raise both attempt and success for fast runners but have little effect on slow runners, so the battery effect scales with runner speed and manager green light.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit attempt hazard with speed x battery interaction; check coefficient on the interaction.

interactions.mechanism: The post-2023 rules (bigger bases, pickoff limits) switched league SB attempt and success levels, and teams differ in how much their managers adapted; a model must reset the baseline at the regime boundary and let manager style scale it.
interactions.how_to_test: Train only on 2023+ data and compare with pooled data; include manager x regime term.

interactions.mechanism: The batter behind a runner affects both RBI opportunity and the steal decision: a strong hitter behind a speedster makes managers less likely to send him early, while a weak batter behind raises steal probability. The lineup order therefore conditions both ladders in opposite ways.
interactions.how_to_test: Add next-batter quality term to steal attempt hazard and RBI opportunity; test sign.

interactions.mechanism: P(2+ RBI) is convex in the game run environment, which here is carried by the team run-scoring opportunity (rbi_opportunity) shifted by park and opposing starter: low-total games almost never produce 2+ while high-total games do so disproportionately. It is convexity, not a threshold, and uses no market total.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute P(2+ RBI) by decile of team run expectation and compare with predictions from a linear opportunity model.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in team scoring: 2+ RBI probability rises faster than expected runners on base
nonlinearities.why: Multiple RBIs require clustered scoring events (HR with runners, two-run hits), so the right tail grows convexly with run environment.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold (approximate, to be fitted): attempt hazard rises sharply above a sprint-speed cutoff, which the author placed near 28 ft/s, and saturates near elite
nonlinearities.why: Stolen-base attempts concentrate among the fastest runners; the response to speed is flat below a threshold and steep above. The 28 ft/s cutoff is an assumption to be estimated from sprint-speed vs attempt-rate data, not an established fact.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex in combined hold time and pop time; the combined-time cutoff (author guess about 3.3 s) is an assumption to be estimated
nonlinearities.why: Steal success is a race against a combined delivery-plus-throw time, which has a sharp advantage zone. The 3.3 s figure is unsourced and depends on time-to-plate data that is not confirmed available.

nonlinearities.shape: Step: moving from slot 3 to slot 5 changes RBI opportunity more than PA because runner volume dominates
nonlinearities.why: PA differences by slot are small, but runner volume per PA rises sharply in the heart of the order, so the effect is nonlinear in slot.

required_data.timestamp_requirement: As-of prior game; catcher and pitcher from lineup card.

candidate_sources.note: Season-grain leaderboards for catcher pop time, runner sprint speed and running game by pitcher/catcher. SOURCE_UNVERIFIED: per-play pop time and a pitcher time-to-plate field are not confirmed to be exposed; proxies are pitcher SB allowed per opportunity and pickoff/lead data.

required_data.fields: ticker, strike, rules text

contract.settlement_definition: Three live series, all with sampled rules. KXMLBGAME pays Yes if the named team wins the listed game; if the game is postponed or delayed the market stays open and closes after the rescheduled game finishes (within two days), and if it is cancelled or rescheduled more than two days away it resolves to a fair price. KXMLBSTGAME (spring-training winner) uses the same winner and postponement wording ('If Cleveland wins the Cleveland vs Arizona professional baseball game originally scheduled for Mar 24, 2026'), but says nothing about a spring game that ends in a tie, which spring rules allow. KXMLBSPREAD pays Yes if the named team wins by more than the stated run margin (e.g. 5.5) in the game originally scheduled for the date, presumably on the final score including extra innings; the sampled KXMLBSPREAD text has no secondary clause, so its postponement and cancellation handling is unstated rather than inherited from KXMLBGAME. None of the texts addresses a suspended game resumed later or a rain-shortened official game. Division, series and All-Star series formerly filed here were moved by the reconciliation. Source of truth is not named.

rules_evidence.quote: If Milwaukee wins by more than 5.5 runs in the Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay professional baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 28, 2026
rules_evidence.establishes: Run spread is 'wins by more than X.5' on the listed game, a threshold on final margin, tied to the game originally scheduled.

rules_evidence.quote: If this game is postponed or delayed, the market will remain open and close after the rescheduled game has finished (within two days).
rules_evidence.establishes: The moneyline survives a postponement of up to two days; the game is then priced as rescheduled, possibly with different starters.

rules_evidence.quote: If the game is cancelled or rescheduled to over two days away, the market will resolve to a fair price in accordance with the rules.
rules_evidence.establishes: Longer postponements and cancellations settle at a fair price rather than voiding at entry.

rules_evidence.quote: If Cleveland wins the Cleveland vs Arizona professional baseball game originally scheduled for Mar 24, 2026 at 3:40 PM EDT, then the market resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: Spring-training winner markets settle on the named team winning; the text has no tie branch even though spring games may end tied.

rules_evidence.quote: If the game is cancelled or rescheduled to over two days away, the market will resolve to a fair price in accordance with the rules.
rules_evidence.establishes: Spring-training markets share the regular-game postponement and fair-price clauses.

variants_and_edge_cases: KXMLBGAME and KXMLBSTGAME wording covers postponement (open up to two days) and cancellation (fair price) but not a suspended game resumed later or a rain-shortened official game; a postponed game that is replayed within two days usually has different probable starters, so the pre-postponement price refers to a different matchup.

Spread strikes are half-runs, so ties after regulation do not matter for the spread; but extra-inning results do (a 1-run walk-off in the 10th gives margin 1), and the margin is of the completed game's final score.

KXMLBSTGAME (spring training, rules sampled): the text pays only if the named team wins and has no tie clause, while spring games can end tied after nine or after limited extra innings; split squads and mass substitutions mean regulars play only the first few innings, so lineup and pitcher inputs carry over only partially (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS, ml_spring_tie).

Postseason single games (the sampled spread is the Oct 28 2026 Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay game, an interleague pairing and therefore a World Series game) differ from regular-season games: no automatic runner in extras, shorter starter hooks, top relievers on consecutive days and elimination-game usage, so the same matchup implies a different margin distribution.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official final scores from MLB (Stats API) for winner and margin; the sampled rules do not name the source.

mechanism.summary: The winner and run margin of a baseball game come from two teams' run processes that interact only through the pitchers, the park and the weather. Each team's runs are the sum over innings of base-out Markov outcomes: the starter pitches the first five or six innings against a nine-man lineup, then relievers cover the remainder with leverage-driven deployment. Run expectation per half-inning is determined by the starter's run prevention and workload, the lineup's strength against his handedness and arsenal, the defense and catcher behind him, the park and weather, and the umpire's zone. The difference of two overdispersed, inning-clustered counts, with a tie after nine resolved by an automatic-runner extra-inning game, gives win probability and the whole margin distribution. Moneyline is therefore a single cut of a distribution that spread rungs read in the tail: margin strikes depend on how often relief teams hold or extend leads and on blowout variance. The edge is concentrated in market-moving information that arrives late (confirmed lineup, scratched starter, roof and wind), and records must be regressed to run-based talent. Spring-training games (KXMLBSTGAME) compress team strength because depth players pitch and bat most innings, and they can end tied, which the contract does not address.

stages.name: Who actually pitches and bats
stages.description: Win probability is conditional on the starting pitchers, the nine batters and the catchers who actually play. Probable starters are announced days ahead but change; lineups post a few hours before first pitch and reflect rest days and platoon choices. Before confirmation the market is a mixture over starter and lineup states, so the information structure is a sequence of announcements rather than a single pregame snapshot.
stages.distribution: Discrete mixture over starter identity (small probability of change) and lineup strength (rest-day sits for regulars cut team strength by a few percent of runs).

stages.name: Team run rates by phase
stages.description: Each team's expected runs are split between the starter's innings and the bullpen's innings. The starter's run prevention (SIERA/xFIP/Stuff+) and expected innings set the weight on starter versus bullpen, the lineup's handedness-specific offence faces the starter's arsenal, and defense and catcher framing adjust balls in play and strikeouts. A better-starter advantage equals the quality gap times expected innings, plus the bullpen gap times the remaining innings.
stages.distribution: Expected runs per team around 3.5-5.5 per game with weighting between starter and bullpen that varies by start (innings ranging from 4 to 7).

stages.name: Environment and officiating
stages.description: Park dimensions and altitude scale run scoring for both teams, with handedness-specific effects; wind and temperature shift carry; the roof can change the day's regime; the umpire's called zone changes walk and strikeout rates for both teams. Home-field advantage is more than constant: last-at-bat advantage and park familiarity matter and vary by park.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative factors on run rates (park factor roughly 0.85 to 1.30); home-field edge a few percentage points of win probability.

stages.name: Run-difference distribution and tie resolution
stages.description: The final margin is a difference of two overdispersed, inning-clustered counts; ties after nine innings go to extra innings: the regular season starts each extra half-inning with an automatic runner on second, but to my knowledge (unverified for 2026) postseason games, which the sampled contracts are, start extras with bases empty, so extras resolve with fewer runs per half-inning and the home team's last-at-bat advantage is the walk-off stopping rule. Margin strikes depend on the skew of this distribution and on bullpen deployment: managers use their best relievers in close games and mop-up arms in blowouts, so winning margins are lumpier than a constant-variance model implies.
stages.distribution: Skellam-like with overdispersion and discrete support; sharp mass at one-run margins; extras resolve ties about even with a home edge.

stages.name: Postseason single-game regime
stages.description: Every sampled contract here is a postseason game, where the state of the series changes the single game: an elimination game pushes managers to use the closer for two innings or a starter on short rest, a team up 3-0 may rest relievers, and travel and off days reset bullpen fatigue. Game win and margin probabilities are therefore conditional on the series state and recent bullpen usage, not only on the listed starters.
stages.distribution: Regime shift in late-inning run prevention (elimination versus non-elimination games); compresses close-game margins and lengthens the one-run tail.

stages.name: Spring-training game regime
stages.description: A spring-training winner depends less on team quality than a regular-season game: starters pitch two to four innings on a ramp-up schedule, regulars leave after a few plate appearances, and the late innings are played by non-roster invitees and minor leaguers whose quality varies widely by club and by split-squad day. Cactus League parks in the Arizona desert inflate scoring relative to Grapefruit League parks, and a game tied after nine may end without a winner, which a literal reading of the winner-only text would settle No for both teams, although no tie clause exists (ml_spring_tie).
stages.distribution: Win probability compressed toward 0.5 (team-strength effect roughly a third of regular season); higher run variance in Arizona parks; a non-trivial tie mass that removes probability from both team markets.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest and travel, regular-season stakes, and postseason series state (elimination leverage) for single games.

mlb.lineup_strength_delta.label: Day-specific lineup strength delta (confirmed lineup vs team baseline, in runs per game)
mlb.lineup_strength_delta.mechanism: The nine hitters who actually play differ from the team's season baseline because of rest days, platoon choices and injuries.
mlb.lineup_strength_delta.rationale: Team-level wRC+ averages across the season's lineups; the confirmed card might lack its best hitter or contain a bench bat, and the effect is not uniform across the order (top slots get more PAs).
mlb.lineup_strength_delta.measurement: delta (runs per game) = sum over slots s of PA_share(s) * (wOBA_proj(hitter_s vs starter hand) - wOBA_proj(baseline_s vs same hand)) / 1.2, where baseline_s = the hitter with the most starts at slot s over the team's last 30 games (PA-weighted if tied) and PA_share = (4.65, 4.55, 4.45, 4.35, 4.25, 4.15, 4.05, 3.95, 3.85), summing to 38.25 PA so no further multiplier is applied. wOBA_proj blends the average of the ZiPS and Steamer ROS projections with 2-season xwOBA shrunk to the projection with k = 300 PA, platoon-adjusted. Units: runs per game (0.100 team-wide wOBA is about 3.2 runs). As-of: lineup post with the projection vintage at that time.
mlb.lineup_strength_delta.why: Late lineup news is the main non-market source of game-level edge and has no explicit measured input in the catalog beyond a data feed.

mlb.home_field_run_advantage.label: Park-specific home-field effect (win-probability and run advantage) with last-at-bat component
mlb.home_field_run_advantage.mechanism: Home teams win more often than road teams: last at-bat, familiarity, travel and umpire exposure.
mlb.home_field_run_advantage.rationale: A constant HFA hides park differences (dimensions, sightlines, altitude familiarity) and the structural last-at-bat advantage that produces extra home wins in tied late innings and truncates the bottom-9th when the home team leads.
mlb.home_field_run_advantage.measurement: Estimate team-home (HFA_t) via mixed model on 10 seasons: run margin ~ team strength (home + away) + home indicator + park random effect (shrunk k = 400 games per park) + travel-days indicator; add last-at-bat component = P(home wins | tied entering 9th) - 0.5 from extras data. Output HFA in run margin and win probability for the specific park. As-of: through prior season plus current.
raw_data: game log: home, away, runs, park, date, innings played
mlb.home_field_run_advantage.why: Distinguishes between parks with large and small HFA, and handles walk-off truncation correctly for margin strikes.

mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.label: Reliever deployment by lead size (who pitches innings 7-9 as a function of margin) and its run-prevention effect
mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.mechanism: Managers use high-leverage relievers in close games and low-leverage arms in blowouts, compressing and lumpifying the margin.
mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.rationale: A margin spread cover is not a symmetric diffusion: leads of one to three runs are protected by the best bullpen arms while four-plus leads are mopped up by weaker arms, so favorites win by exactly one or two more often than a normal model suggests.
mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.measurement: For each team over the last 2 seasons: runs allowed per inning in innings 7-9 by lead bucket (tie/within1, 2-3, 4+) and by reliever tier (top-3 by leverage index vs rest). Shrink bucket runs allowed to league with k = 100 innings. Combine with the margin distribution through a Markov simulation in innings 7-9: P(margin change | state). Units: run-allowed rate by state. As-of: bullpen availability at lineup post.
free_sources: MLB Stats API play-by-play (leverage index, pitching changes)
raw_data: inning-level: team, inning, score diff, pitcher used, leverage index, runs allowed
mlb.late_inning_leverage_deployment.why: Distribution tail for run-line and margin contracts, as sketched in the existing run_dist hypothesis but without a measured input.

mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.label: Regular-season stakes and rest policy (clinched/eliminated status, rest-day probabilities, September roster behaviour)
mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.mechanism: Teams that have clinched or been eliminated rest regulars, shorten starters' leashes or run tryout lineups, which lowers team strength on that day relative to the full-strength baseline.
mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.rationale: Late-season games for clinched or eliminated teams are played by different hitters and a differently managed bullpen than the season-long ratings assume; lineup_strength_delta only sees this after the card posts, while starter handling and bullpen usage in meaningless games never flow through it. Postseason games have no such effect, so the input must be gated by game type.
mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.measurement: For each team-game compute (a) playoff-clinch and elimination flags from standings (magic number <= games remaining, or tragic number), (b) games_since_last_rest_day for each of the 9 regular-lineup hitters and their historical P(sit) when the team is clinched/eliminated/in a day-game-after-night-game, estimated over the prior 5 seasons with shrinkage k = 40 team-games, (c) starter innings expectation reduced by the team's historical clinched/eliminated leash shift. Output: expected regular-lineup PA share and expected starter innings; units are PA share and innings. As-of: the morning of the game, updated at lineup post. Set to neutral for postseason games.
free_sources: MLB Stats API standings and schedule
mlb.regular_season_stakes_and_rest_polic.why: Fills the regular-season motivation gap for KXMLBGAME-type contracts (late-season starts, rested regulars) that rest_travel and series_context do not address.

mlb.spring_training_playing_time_regime.label: Spring-training playing-time regime: share of innings and plate appearances by MLB regulars versus non-roster and minor-league players, split-squad flag and tie rule
mlb.spring_training_playing_time_regime.mechanism: Spring-game outcomes depend on who plays the late innings, which is set by ramp-up schedules, split squads and the number of non-roster players each club carries, not by regular-season talent.
mlb.spring_training_playing_time_regime.rationale: KXMLBSTGAME settles on a spring game, where regulars play perhaps a third of the innings and the rest goes to depth players of uneven quality; a club playing a split-squad game sends a weaker roster, and spring games may end tied, so regular-season ratings mislead without this adjustment.
mlb.spring_training_playing_time_regime.measurement: For each club and game: expected innings share of 40-man players = sum over announced pitchers of planned innings / 9 and over the posted lineup of expected PA share (regulars about 2 PA, then substitutes); quality of the remainder from projected minor-league equivalents (wOBA and FIP) shrunk toward replacement with k = 100 PA; split-squad flag from the schedule; tie rate by league (Cactus, Grapefruit) from 2015-2026 spring results. Team strength for the game = innings-share-weighted average of regular and depth ratings. As-of: posted spring lineup and probable pitchers; units: run-value per game.
free_sources: MLB.com spring-training lineups and box scores (free_scrape)
raw_data: spring-training box scores with innings by pitcher and PA by batter
mlb.spring_training_playing_time_regime.why: KXMLBSTGAME requires a team-strength measure for the players who actually play spring innings and the tie probability the contract does not address.

mlb.sp_quality.reason: Largest single determinant of expected runs; requires projection-based blend and regression, with scratch-risk.

mlb.sp_workload.reason: Starter weight versus bullpen; innings distribution not mean matters.

mlb.team_wrc_vs_hand.reason: Hand-specific lineup offence versus starter; team-level proxy replaced by lineup_strength_delta for the day.

mlb.lineup_pit.reason: Confirmation changes the answer; vintage required.

mlb.bullpen.reason: Availability and fatigue shift late-inning run prevention; useful with decay on last 3 days usage.

mlb.bullpen_talent.reason: Reliever quality sets the remaining 3-4 innings; true talent unstable, use projections.

mlb.defense.reason: OAA and framing influence BABIP and K/BB; the label bundles two effects.

mlb.park.reason: Park factor scales both teams symmetrically so moves total more than winner; matters for margin strikes.

mlb.weather_pit.reason: Weather scales run environment and affects totals more than win probability.

mlb.umpire.reason: Small symmetric effect on both teams' scoring; limited relevance to winner.

mlb.injuries_pit.reason: Late scratches and IL changes drive confirmed-card differences; timing matters.

mlb.rest_travel.reason: Effects on win probability are small and mostly flow through who rests; check for day-after-night-game rest. It is no longer the only schedule input: regular_season_stakes_and_rest_policy covers clinched/eliminated rest behaviour.

mlb.pythag_luck.reason: Regress record luck to run-differential-based talent; important for futures and series.

mlb.run_dist.reason: Determines margin tails and tie mass; needs inning-level dispersion and correlation with park.

mlb.extra_innings.reason: Tie resolution matters in about nine percent of games for moneyline; directional for spreads.

mlb.opp_strength.reason: Single-game ratings already carry opponent adjustment inside the run-based components (sp_quality, team_wrc_vs_hand), so it is redundant there; kept as secondary only for the team-level latent strength used in series and division aggregation, where schedule strength differs.

m.external_lines.reason: Sharp sportsbook lines are a benchmark for fair probability, not an information source; catalog's 'secondary' role is a category error.

m.quote_history.reason: Price movement after lineup news is market response; use for evaluation of timeliness, not as input.

m.rules_text.reason: KXMLBGAME's two-day postponement window and fair-price cancellation, the spread's final-score margin and the unseen spring-training tie rule decide what is priced; wording must be versioned per series.

mlb.platoon.reason: Lineup handedness mix against the starter is already inside hand-specific team offence.

mlb.pitch_mix.reason: Pitch-mix effects on strikeouts are not an input to winning probability beyond what SIERA/Stuff+ already summarises.

mlb.lineup_k_platoon.reason: Confirmed-lineup K% by hand is a strikeout-market summary; run scoring needs wOBA-level not K-only matchups.

interactions.mechanism: The effective pitching edge is the starter quality gap times the share of innings he covers plus the bullpen gap times the rest, so starter workload acts as a weight that changes with the specific starter and with postseason leashes. A better starter who goes five innings counts for less than the same gap over seven.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute innings-weighted pitching rating versus separate terms; compare win-probability log loss on postseason versus regular season.

interactions.mechanism: Confirmed-lineup changes matter conditional on the starter's hand and the slot of the missing hitter: a left-handed bat resting against a lefty starter is no loss, while a missing right-handed regular against a lefty is. The same absence has different run value by matchup.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact missing-hitter value with starter hand and slot; test whether the delta is better modelled with hand-specific projections.

interactions.mechanism: Home advantage concentrates in the late innings: home teams skip the bottom 9th when ahead and win tied games by last bat, so HFA enters margin strikes as truncation and win probability as a tie-resolution bonus, not as a uniform shift in run difference.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate HFA separately for innings 1-8 and 9+ from historical run margins; check effect on spread rungs.

interactions.mechanism: Large margins are compressed because trailing teams' pitchers are replaced with weaker arms only after the game is out of reach, while narrow leads are protected; the probability of covering a 1.5-run spread is therefore not monotone with a constant-variance model, and fatigued bullpens loosen the compression.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare spread-rung calibration for favorites by bullpen freshness and lead bucket.

interactions.mechanism: In a postseason single game the series state switches bullpen and starter usage: in elimination games the best relievers pitch more and earlier and starters are pulled at the first sign of trouble, so a starter-quality edge counts for fewer innings and the late-inning margin distribution tightens; in non-elimination games of a lopsided series usage relaxes.
interactions.how_to_test: Backtest series winner probabilities from sequential game models versus constant single-game probability.

interactions.mechanism: In spring the announced starter's quality matters only for his planned two to four innings, after which depth arms of unknown quality pitch; the effect of a better starter on win probability is therefore cut off at his innings limit, unlike the regular season where an ace's influence extends six or more innings.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress spring game outcomes on starter quality interacted with planned innings and compare the slope with the regular-season slope.

nonlinearities.shape: Logistic-like win probability in expected run difference (about 10% per run near evenly matched), with Pythagorean exponent near 1.8 concave in run ratio
nonlinearities.why: Win probability is a concave-then-saturating function of expected run difference, so large favorites gain progressively less per added run of edge.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating weight: the incremental weight on the starter flattens beyond about 6 innings
nonlinearities.why: The starter's share of innings is bounded and hooks are sharp, so adding workload past six innings adds little to team run prevention.

nonlinearities.shape: Regression coefficient falls with games played; partial pooling toward run-differential talent
nonlinearities.why: The reliability of record versus run-differential grows slowly, so shrinkage weights should depend on sample size nonlinearly.

nonlinearities.shape: Multiplicative scaling of run rate with dispersion scaling (variance rises with park factor)
nonlinearities.why: Hitter-friendly parks raise both the mean and variance of runs, which matters for margin tails.

contract.settlement_definition: Two live series with sampled rules: KXMLBTOTAL pays Yes if the two teams collectively score more than the strike (e.g. 8.5 runs, text 'collectively score more 8.5 runs') in the listed game; KXMLBTEAMTOTAL pays Yes if the named team scores N or more runs (title 'over 7.5', rule '8+'). The sampled rules do not state whether extra-inning runs count, whether an unplayed bottom of the ninth changes anything, or how postponed, suspended and rain-shortened games settle. The series-length markets formerly filed here moved to the playoff-series archetype. Source of truth is not named.

rules_evidence.quote: collectively score more 8.5 runs in the Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay professional baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 28, 2026
rules_evidence.establishes: Game total is a combined-runs threshold on the listed game (note wording omits 'than'); sampled text does not mention extra innings.

rules_evidence.quote: If Tampa Bay scores 8+ runs in the Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay professional baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 28, 2026
rules_evidence.establishes: Team total strike is an 'N+' on one team (title says over 7.5 but the rule says 8+), a discrete tail event.

rules_evidence.quote: Will Tampa Bay score over 7.5 runs?
rules_evidence.establishes: The title states a half-run strike while the rule says '8+', the same event (8 or more runs).

variants_and_edge_cases: Whether extra-inning runs count toward game and team totals is not stated in the sample (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS); the existing catalog assumes they do, but the settlement text is silent.
When the home team leads after 8.5 innings the bottom of the ninth is not played, truncating both the game total and the home team total relative to a nine-inning-per-side expectation.
Team total wording differs between title (over 7.5) and rule (8+): the rule text governs and both describe 8 or more runs.
Postponed or suspended games remain tied to the 'originally scheduled' game, but the sample gives no explicit treatment.

Both sampled totals are October postseason games: MLB's automatic extra-innings runner applies to the regular season only, so postseason extras add runs at roughly the bases-empty late-inning rate and a regular-season total with the same pregame expectation has a fatter extras tail.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official game score (MLB Stats API / box score) for game and team totals; source not named in the sampled rules.

mechanism.summary: Total runs are the sum of two teams' runs, each the sum over innings of a clustered run process. For a team, expected runs equal the opposing starter's run prevention over the innings he covers plus the bullpen's rate over the rest, applied to the lineup's strength against that starter's hand and arsenal, then scaled multiplicatively by park, wind, air density and the umpire's zone, with defense adjusting balls in play. The distribution is overdispersed because runs cluster in big innings that start from baserunners and are amplified by home runs and relievers entering. Totals are therefore not a symmetric band around a mean: thresholds near the median price the shape of the right tail, which depends on environment (Coors, wind blowing out) that changes variance as well as the mean. Structural details matter: the home team's bottom of the ninth is not played when it leads, extra innings add runs (with an automatic runner) if the contract counts them, and a postponed or shortened game changes the sum. Series-length markets left this archetype and are not generated here.

stages.name: Pitching matchup and workload
stages.description: Runs allowed by each pitching staff come first from the listed starter and how long he pitches, then from the relievers who finish. The starter's true-talent run prevention, innings expectation and the manager's leash determine the split, and a scratch of the listed starter changes the total by a large amount. Bullpen availability changes late-inning rates.
stages.distribution: Mixture over starter exit time (4-7 innings) and over bullpen composition; scratch risk as rare regime.

stages.name: Lineup offence and matchup
stages.description: Each team's offence is the confirmed nine facing the specific starter: handedness-specific wRC+, order slot weights, and contact quality versus the starter's profile. Defense and catcher framing shape balls in play and strikeouts on the pitching side.
stages.distribution: Per-team expected runs about 3.5-5.5 with sd of expectation uncertainty about 0.4 runs from lineup and starter information.

stages.name: Run-environment multipliers
stages.description: Park factors, altitude, wind direction relative to the park axis, temperature and humidity (air density), roof state, ball regime and the umpire's called zone scale run scoring multiplicatively; the day-specific deviation from park norms is the information, because the park average is already priced. Variance increases with run environment.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative on mean runs (about 0.85-1.35); heteroskedastic: variance grows with the environment.

stages.name: Run distribution, truncation and extras
stages.description: Realised totals are drawn from an overdispersed, inning-clustered distribution. The home team may not bat in the ninth; a tie after nine brings extra innings, which in the regular season start each half-inning with an automatic runner on second (about one run per half-inning) but in the postseason start with the bases empty (roughly half that), and those runs matter only if the contract counts them. The right tail of the total thresholds (10+ runs) is driven by big innings and weak-bullpen blowups.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed discrete (negative-binomial-like) per team, correlated positively across teams via shared park and weather; truncated by bottom-9 skip and extended by extras.

stages.name: Postseason run-environment regime
stages.description: The sampled totals are from the Oct 28 2026 Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay World Series game (an interleague pairing), where run scoring follows a different regime from the regular season: starters are pulled earlier but replaced by the best relievers rather than long men, cold October weather in northern parks suppresses carry, rotations shorten to the top three or four starters, and extras have no automatic runner. Game and team totals must be priced with postseason-specific starter and bullpen splits rather than regular-season team averages.
stages.distribution: Downward shift of the total's mean and a thinner right tail relative to a regular-season game with the same listed starters; extras contribution roughly halved.

distribution_variance.note: Overdispersion of the inning-clustered run count plus truncation of the home half-innings by the walk-off rule.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Postseason bullpen and starter usage regime for the sampled October games; regular-season rest and travel act through the confirmed lineup and bullpen inputs.

coaching_scheme.note: Manager strategy (bunting, intentional walks, pitching changes) has effects on run scoring that are second-order relative to pitchers, lineups and park; no sampled contract wording interacts with a managerial rule in a way that changes the count of runs, and the leash effect is included under workload.

mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.label: Probability the home team's bottom of the ninth is skipped (home lead after 8.5) and its run-total effect
mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.mechanism: A home team ahead after the top of the ninth does not bat, so its runs and the game total are truncated relative to nine full innings.
mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.rationale: A total of 8.5 is often priced as if both teams bat nine innings; in games where the home team is ahead the home runs stop early, shifting probability toward under, and the truncation is correlated with favorite status and low total.
mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.measurement: Take P(home skips bottom 9) = P(home leads after the top of the 9th) from mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher (not recomputed). Combined-total truncation loss = P(skip) * mu9, mu9 = the home team's expected runs in a full bottom-9 half inning (about 0.5, estimated from half-inning data 2015-2025 with team shrinkage k = 100 half-innings). Walk-off truncation: when the home team trails by d or is tied entering the bottom 9th or later, the half ends when it takes the lead, so its expected runs = E[min(runs, d+1)] with the exception that a home run counts every run on the play, computed from a base-out Markov chain with the team's PA outcome rates. Apply the loss to the home team total and the combined total, not to the visitor total. Output expected truncation in runs for home total, visitor total and combined total. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: linescore: runs by inning by team, innings played, home flag
half-inning base-out data for stopping-rule simulation
mlb.bottom_ninth_truncation.why: Directly changes total thresholds near the median, especially for strong home favorites, and is absent from the existing catalog.

mlb.extras_run_contribution.label: Expected runs added by extra innings, by rule regime (regular-season automatic runner vs postseason bases-empty) and contract scope
mlb.extras_run_contribution.mechanism: A game tied after nine adds extra half-innings; in the regular season each starts with a runner on second, in the postseason (to my knowledge, unverified for 2026) each starts with bases empty, so the runs added differ by regime; runs there count only if the contract counts them.
mlb.extras_run_contribution.rationale: About one game in ten adds a few runs, which matters for rungs near the median; if the contract excludes extras, then these runs must be removed and shortened-game and walk-off logic differ.
mlb.extras_run_contribution.measurement: E[extras runs] = P(level after nine complete innings) x E[total runs in extras | level]. Estimate runs per extra half-inning by regime: regular season with automatic runner (2020-2025 extras, about 0.9-1.1 runs per half-inning, shrunk to team offence with k = 50 half-innings); postseason or any bases-empty extras at about the league per-inning rate for tied late-inning bullpens (about 0.45-0.55 runs per half-inning, estimated from postseason and pre-2020 extra innings). The home half ends at the go-ahead run (walk-off stopping rule), so the home half contributes fewer runs than the visitor half. Use the regime flag from the game type (regular season vs postseason) and set to 0 if rules say regulation only. Units: expected runs. As-of: lineup post and contract text version.
free_sources: Retrosheet / MLB Stats API extra-inning data
mlb.extras_run_contribution.why: The existing catalog assumes extras count but the sampled rules are silent; the input keeps the dependence explicit and testable. Re-specified by regime because all sampled totals are postseason games, where the automatic runner is not used to my knowledge.

mlb.series_length_distribution.label: Series length distribution (probability of 4/5/6/7 games) from game-level win probabilities with team-strength dependence
mlb.series_length_distribution.mechanism: A series total contract settles on how many games are played, a function of game win probabilities, home-field pattern and the dependence of games on a shared team-strength latent.
mlb.series_length_distribution.rationale: Using independent Bernoulli games understates the probability of sweeps and long series; team strength uncertainty and starter rotation make the sequence dependent, and short series compress the talent gap.
mlb.series_length_distribution.measurement: Simulate best-of-seven: game i win prob p_i from the single-game model with announced starters and rest (default 2-3-2 home pattern), draw team-strength offset ~ N(0, sd = 0.04 in win prob) shared across games, compute P(N=4,5,6,7). P(7 games)=1 - P(<=6). Calibrate sd to historical series length frequency (best-of-7 series since 2012). As-of: after each game with updated series state.
free_sources: Game-level win probability from team model
raw_data: per-game pregame win probability from the project's model
mlb.series_length_distribution.why: Defined here while KXMLBSERIESGAMES was filed in this archetype; that series now belongs to the playoff-series archetype and this input is no longer staged here.

mlb.sp_workload.reason: Innings split between starter and bullpen; distribution matters.

mlb.bullpen.reason: Availability and fatigue affect late-inning runs; decays over 3 days.

mlb.bullpen_talent.reason: Reliever quality sets the late-inning rate; unstable and heteroskedastic.

mlb.team_wrc_vs_hand.reason: Confirmed-lineup hand-specific offence is the primary offensive input.

mlb.lineup_pit.reason: Confirmed card replaces probable lineup; vintage matters.

mlb.park.reason: Strongest stable multiplier of runs; use park by handedness.

mlb.weather_pit.reason: Raw weather bundle: its wind component is the park-relative wind in wind_vector_park, its temperature/humidity are in air_density.

mlb.wind_vector_park.reason: Wind component relative to park axis; expressed as deviation from park norm.

mlb.air_density.reason: Density deviation from park mean; sizeable at altitude and in heat.

mlb.roof_state.reason: Roof open or closed gates wind and weather; decision timing uncertain.

mlb.umpire.reason: Called zone changes run scoring modestly; late information.

mlb.contact_defense.reason: Contact allowed and defense; partially duplicated by sp_quality (SIERA/xFIP).

mlb.defense.reason: Defensive runs saved shift BABIP; mostly captured in pitching run-prevention metrics.

mlb.babip_luck.reason: Regression of BABIP luck in team samples; only matters when ratings are built from raw results.

mlb.rule_regime.reason: League run baselines shift between seasons with rule and ball changes; recalibrate each season.

mlb.run_dist.reason: Dispersion and tail shape price the thresholds; must be modelled per environment.

mlb.extra_innings.reason: Extra-inning rules matter only if the contract counts extras and for P(tie after nine).

m.ladder_structure.reason: Cross-rung price consistency is a market-derived diagnostic and not an input.

m.rules_text.reason: Treatment of extras, shortened games and series counting is unspecified and decides what is being priced.

interactions.mechanism: Park factor, wind and air density multiply the same fly-ball carry, so in a hitter's park with a tailwind and thin air the effects compound; deviations from park norms, not absolute weather, carry the information, and the effect is largest for fly-ball-heavy lineups and starters.
interactions.how_to_test: Model run multiplier as park x exp(beta_wind*wind_dev + beta_air*density_dev) and compare with additive terms.

interactions.mechanism: The total is a mixture of starter-run and bullpen-run innings, so the sensitivity of the total to starter quality depends on how long he goes, which depends on bullpen state and leash. A depleted bullpen lengthens the leash and thereby increases weight on the starter's quality.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact starter quality with exit-time distribution and bullpen freshness; check total residual by those terms.

interactions.mechanism: A smaller called zone raises walks and run scoring most for patient lineups against command-poor pitchers, and a larger zone helps pitchers with edge-heavy approach; umpire effect scales with the matchup's walk exposure rather than adding a fixed number of runs.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact umpire zone residual with lineup chase rate and pitcher zone rate in a walk model; test total residuals.

interactions.mechanism: In high-run environments variance rises faster than the mean (clustering of crooked-number innings), so the probability of totals above the model median falls less than a constant-variance model implies, and the under side is more exposed at low thresholds.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate dispersion as a function of park factor and wind-out indicator; compare calibration of thresholds near 10 runs in Coors versus pitcher's parks.

interactions.mechanism: Game-length regime: when the home team leads, the bottom of the ninth is skipped (negative total adjustment); when tied, extras add runs; when the home team trails, the game runs to completion. The three regimes sit at different parts of the run-difference distribution, so the expected total is a mixture with different slopes.
interactions.how_to_test: Condition historical totals on score state after eight innings and compare to unconditional total model.

nonlinearities.shape: Overdispersed negative-binomial tail: P(total >= 11) is several times a Poisson prediction
nonlinearities.why: Runs cluster in innings and crooked numbers amplify, so the right tail is heavy relative to a Poisson with the same mean; thresholds are priced in the tail.

nonlinearities.shape: Asymmetric saturating: out-blowing wind adds more carry than in-blowing wind removes, both saturate beyond about 15 mph
nonlinearities.why: Carry gains and losses at the wall are not symmetric and flatten at high wind speeds.

nonlinearities.shape: Roughly linear in density for HR carry, convex for hit-by-hit effects at altitude
nonlinearities.why: Reduced drag accumulates over a long flight, so the benefit rises more in the far outfield; Coors differs qualitatively.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex penalty for poor starters: a bad starter's extra runs per inning are larger because bullpen exposure grows and leverage rises
nonlinearities.why: A weak starter exits early, exposing the bullpen and raising run totals more than his rate gap alone suggests.
