contract.settlement_definition: Five live series, all with sampled rules, now filed here: KXMLBF5, KXMLBF3 and KXMLBF7 (winner of the first 5/3/7 innings with a 'Tie' strike: if the score at the end of the named inning is tied the Tie strike resolves Yes and all team strikes No), KXMLBF5SPREAD (named team wins the first five innings by more than a margin, e.g. 2.5) and KXMLBF5TOTAL (combined runs in the first five innings more than a strike, e.g. 6.5). All say a postponed or delayed game keeps the market open and it closes after the rescheduled game finishes (within two days). No pitcher clause appears, so a starter change does not void. A game called before the named inning completes is not addressed. Source of truth is not named.

rules_evidence.quote: If the score at the end of the first 5 innings is tied, the "Tie" strike will resolve to Yes and all team strikes will resolve to No.
rules_evidence.establishes: The F5 winner market is three-way with an explicit Tie strike.

rules_evidence.quote: If this game is postponed or delayed, the market will remain open and close after the rescheduled game has finished (within two days).
rules_evidence.establishes: Postponed or delayed games keep the market open for up to two days rather than voiding.

rules_evidence.quote: collectively score more than 6.5 runs in the first 5 innings
rules_evidence.establishes: The total counts combined runs through five innings, a half-run strike with no tie branch.

rules_evidence.quote: If the score at the end of the first 3 innings is tied
rules_evidence.establishes: The same Tie-strike construction applies to the three-inning variant.

rules_evidence.quote: If Milwaukee and Tampa Bay tie in the first 7 innings
rules_evidence.establishes: The seven-inning variant exists with rules text, so bullpen innings enter the cumulative score.

variants_and_edge_cases: INFERENCE (no pitcher clause appears in the sampled rules, so silence is read as no void): a changed or scratched starter is assumed not to void the F5 market, so starter-change risk is priced rather than refunded, unlike the player-prop ladders. Not confirmed by any explicit rule.
Winner markets have three strikes (each team and Tie); spread and total markets have no tie strike, so a tied score after five matters differently across the three contracts.
A game called before the fifth inning is complete (rain) is not addressed in the sampled text (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS); 'delayed' games stay open for up to two days.
Related strikes exist for 3 and 7 innings (KXMLBF3, KXMLBF7), which shift weight between starter and bullpen.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official linescore at the end of the third, fifth and seventh innings (MLB Stats API / box score) for F3, F5/F5SPREAD/F5TOTAL and F7; not named in the sampled rules.

mechanism.summary: Runs in the first five innings are produced almost entirely by the two starters and their lineups, with the bullpen entering only after an early exit. Each starter faces the opposing order roughly twice, so the first five innings weight the top six hitters of each lineup more heavily than a nine-inning game does, and the times-through-the-order penalty applies across the second trip. The expected score per team is therefore the starter's run prevention over an exit-time distribution (an early pull exposes relievers) against the confirmed lineup by handedness, scaled by the park, weather and the umpire's zone, which is more influential early. Because the half-inning run process is clustered and discrete, five-inning margins are lumpy and ties are frequent enough that the winner, spread and total contracts differ materially: the winner market has a Tie strike, the spread a margin, the total a sum. Bullpen strength matters less than in the full game; starter leash and opener usage matter more. The sampled rules do not void a starter change, so late scratches are priced risk.

stages.name: Listed starters and change risk
stages.description: Because the contract is not conditioned on the pitcher, the starter announced earlier might be replaced by another starter or an opener at any time before first pitch, and the market sits on the pre-announcement distribution until the lineup confirms. The distribution over actual starters is the first stage; its variance is large in postseason and when the listed pitcher is on a minor injury.
stages.distribution: Discrete mixture over starter identity with rare but high-impact switches; resolved at lineup post and first pitch.

stages.name: Starter run prevention across two trips
stages.description: Over the first five innings the starter faces the order about twice, and some starters a third time. Run prevention per trip falls for most pitchers on the second look, with a larger penalty for pitchers with few pitch types, while pitchers who exit before the fifth hand innings to relievers with a different rate. The mix over exit times is the key distribution.
stages.distribution: Mixture over exit time (about 4-6.5 innings); trip-specific run rates with second-trip penalty.

stages.name: Lineup slots weighted by first-five exposure
stages.description: In five innings each team sends about 21-23 batters to the plate, so slots 1-4 bat twice and often slots 5-6 twice if the offence is productive, while slots 7-9 are weighted less. The confirmed order and its handedness against the starter determine the weight on each hitter's skill set, and platoon advantages of the top of the order dominate.
stages.distribution: Slot exposure weights from a Markov chain; top-6 weight roughly 2/3 of PAs.

stages.name: Environment and zone early in the game
stages.description: Park dimensions, altitude, wind, temperature and the roof scale run scoring from the first pitch, and the plate umpire's zone is a large early-game effect because the early innings are pitched by the starters; contact quality and defense (balls in play) shape hits allowed.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative factor on run rate with higher variance in hitter-friendly parks; umpire effect about a few percent of runs.

stages.name: Discrete score distribution and tie mass
stages.description: The five-inning score is a pair of discrete overdispersed counts; the tie probability (about one game in eight) is the sum over equal scores and is sensitive to the total: low-total games tie more. The three contracts read this distribution differently (Tie strike, margin strikes, total strikes), so the model must output the full joint PMF.
stages.distribution: Skellam-like with extra clustering; tie mass concentrated at 0-0, 1-1, 2-2.

stages.name: Three- and seven-inning windows
stages.description: KXMLBF3 settles after three innings, so it is almost entirely the two starters' first trip through the order against the top of each lineup, with first-inning scoring weighting heavily. KXMLBF7 adds innings six and seven, which most starters do not finish: the result depends on each bullpen's quality and availability after recent usage and on managers' leverage choices when leading or trailing late, so the F7 tie mass and margin are shaped by middle relief rather than starters.
stages.distribution: F3: low totals with tie mass near 0.3 (0-0 and 1-1 dominate); F7: cumulative scores close to full-game shape with tie mass around 0.12, mixed over bullpen availability states.

talent_strength.note: Starter run prevention with luck regression.

pace_volume.note: Starter share of the five innings.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest and clinched-seed effects shape which starters and regulars play but are already carried by starter identity and the confirmed lineup; no schedule or motivation factor changes five-inning run scoring beyond those, so there is no separate driver for this contract.

mlb.f5_starter_change_risk.label: Probability the listed starter does not start (scratch, opener, bulk swap) and replacement distribution
mlb.f5_starter_change_risk.mechanism: Contracts that do not gate on the pitcher (F5 lines, opposing-hitter props) stay live when the listed starter is scratched or swapped, so the change probability and the replacement's identity shift the whole outcome distribution.
mlb.f5_starter_change_risk.rationale: Pre-lineup prices sit on the announced pitcher; a late scratch or opener plan is a large run-expectation change (a quality starter replaced by a bullpen day), and in the postseason pitching plans change.
mlb.f5_starter_change_risk.measurement: P(change) = logistic(a + b1*days_to_first_pitch + b2*IL_return_flag + b3*injury_report_flag + b4*team opener or bulk start rate in last 10 starts + b5*postseason + b6*doubleheader), fitted only on own-captured announced-versus-actual starters; until at least one full season of captured vintages exists, use the league base rate stratified by status flags with a Beta prior (k = 100 games) and label the output uncalibrated. Replacement distribution = mixture of next-in-rotation, bulk reliever and opener with their F5 run rates over 2 seasons shrunk to team average with k = 8 starts. Output P(change), the replacement distribution (identity, throwing hand and role of each candidate with probabilities), E[F5 runs | change] minus E[F5 runs | no change] for F5 markets, and the replacement mixture used by opposing-hitter props through mlb.pitcher_hr_vulnerability. As-of: each timestamp before first pitch, using only announcements available then.
free_sources: MLB Stats API probable pitchers history (vintage unverified)
mlb.f5_starter_change_risk.why: Without a refund clause the change risk is not hedged; it is a primary driver of early-market error.

mlb.f5_lineup_slot_exposure.label: Expected plate appearances by slot in innings 1-5 and slot-weighted matchup runs
mlb.f5_lineup_slot_exposure.mechanism: Within five innings the top of each order bats twice and the bottom less, so slots receive unequal weight.
mlb.f5_lineup_slot_exposure.rationale: Full-game wRC+ weights nine slots roughly evenly; F5 weight shifts toward the top six, and the weight on the top varies with team OBP (more baserunners, more PAs).
mlb.f5_lineup_slot_exposure.measurement: Markov-chain expected PA by slot in 5 innings given lineup OBP and starter allowed OBP: roughly (2.75, 2.65, 2.6, 2.5, 2.4, 2.3, 2.2, 2.1, 2.0) for a typical team, which sums to the team total of about 21.5 PA in five innings (about 4.3 PA per inning); slot weights are normalised to sum to the modelled team PA total. Slot-weighted runs per PA = sum slot weight x hitter run value vs starter hand (projection wOBA, k = 300 PA shrinkage). Units: expected runs in 5 innings against a typical starter. As-of: lineup post.
mlb.f5_lineup_slot_exposure.why: Converts the confirmed lineup into five-inning exposure rather than a nine-inning average.

mlb.f5_reliever_innings_share.label: Expected share of the first five innings thrown by relievers (early exit) and their quality
mlb.f5_reliever_innings_share.mechanism: Early starter exits push relievers into innings 4 and 5; the mixture shifts F5 runs.
mlb.f5_reliever_innings_share.rationale: Starter-only models understate runs when the starter has a short leash, and bullpen quality (not starter) then governs the end of the F5 window; openers make the share large.
mlb.f5_reliever_innings_share.measurement: From the shared starter exit hazard mlb.sp_hook_hazard_curve compute E[outs by reliever in innings 1-5] = 15 - E[min(starter outs, 15)]; relief quality from the likely first reliever and leverage; F5 reliever share = that/15. F5 runs = starter rate x share_starter + reliever rate x share_relief. Uses 5 seasons start logs, k = 8 starts shrinkage to team average. Units: outs and runs per out. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: start-level: outs by starter, relievers entering, run rates
mlb.f5_reliever_innings_share.why: F5 differs from full game in how much bullpen enters; this is the explicit mixture weight.

mlb.f3_split.label: First-three-innings run split and top-of-order exposure by lineup
mlb.f3_split.mechanism: The first three innings give every starter a full turn through the top of the order and are mostly pitcher-quality and lineup-top dependent.
mlb.f3_split.rationale: Early-innings markets depend on the starter at full strength and lineup order exposure; the bullpen is rarely involved. Subtle: only one pass through the order mostly, so TTO penalty is irrelevant but first-inning splits are noisy.
mlb.f3_split.measurement: Simulate innings 1-3 for each team using the confirmed batting order and the chain in mlb.pa_base_out_state_chain: PA outcome probabilities by log5 of the hitter's rates versus starter hand (shrunk to projections with k = 250 PA) and the opposing starter's first-time-through-order PA outcome rates (2 seasons, shrunk to league with k = 300 BF), adjusted for park and weather. Run 20,000 simulations or solve the chain analytically. Output the run distribution for innings 1-3 per team, expected PA, and the ratio E[F3 runs]/E[F5 runs] versus the league ratio. As-of: lineup post.
free_sources: Baseball Savant / pybaseball statcast (baseballsavant.mlb.com/statcast_search CSV export, leaderboards)
raw_data: PA-level outcomes by batter and pitcher
mlb.f3_split.why: KXMLBF3 (filed here) settles on the innings 1-3 result, so the starter's first-trip run split by confirmed lineup is the core window input for the three-inning market.

mlb.sp_quality.reason: Starter run prevention drives the market; needs trip-specific rates not a season average.

mlb.f5_split.reason: Team-level F5-versus-bullpen split is useful as a shrink target but confounds starter quality and bullpen quality.

mlb.leash.reason: Manager hook tendency has no estimand of its own; its content (manager random effect, bullpen freshness, pitch-count and run-state triggers) is a component of the one shared starter exit-hazard model sp_hook_hazard_curve, and the catalog definition of leash is patched to say so.

mlb.tto.reason: Second-look penalty and third-trip exposure inside five innings are core to F5.

mlb.team_wrc_vs_hand.reason: Lineup versus starter hand is the core offensive input; team-level, replaced by slot-weighted version.

mlb.lineup_pit.reason: Confirmed order sets slot exposure; vintage matters.

mlb.platoon.reason: The handedness composition is already in hand-specific team offence.

mlb.park.reason: Scale of run environment by hand; affects both teams.

mlb.weather_pit.reason: Weather scales early scoring modestly; effect mostly through park norm deviations.

mlb.umpire.reason: Zone more influential early when starters pitch; late information.

mlb.contact_defense.reason: Contact quality allowed and defense; partially captured in sp_quality.

mlb.run_dist.reason: Needed for tie mass and margin PMF in five innings; five-inning dispersion differs from nine.

mlb.bullpen.reason: Only relevant after an early exit; use via f5_reliever_innings_share.

m.rules_text.reason: Tie strike, two-day postponement window and the absence of a pitcher clause differ from the player-prop wording and define what is priced; versions must be tracked per series (F3, F5, F7, spread, total).

mlb.lob_strand_luck.reason: Strand luck regression matters when ratings use ERA; use FIP-type estimators instead.

interactions.mechanism: F5 run rate is a mixture of starter-only innings and starter-plus-reliever innings: a good starter with a short leash pushes relievers into the fifth, while a mediocre starter with a long leash keeps them out, so the expected value depends on exit probability times the quality gap between starter and reliever.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit F5 runs on mixture weights from the exit hazard; compare residual by starter exit tercile.

interactions.mechanism: Because slots 1-4 bat twice within five innings, platoon advantage at the top of the order is weighted more than in a full game; a lefty-heavy top four against a righty starter inflates F5 runs by more than the team-level wRC+ suggests. Tested at slot level as batter handedness (from the confirmed card) crossed with the starter hand, weighted by expected first-five PA, rather than against the duplicate platoon team aggregate.
interactions.how_to_test: Contrast F5 runs for lineups whose slots 1-4 are platoon-advantaged against the starter hand versus those whose slots 5-9 are, holding total team wRC+ vs hand fixed.

interactions.mechanism: The second-trip penalty arrives at about the 10th batter and is larger for pitchers with narrow arsenals, so the effect is discontinuous in batters faced and has a pitcher-specific size; strand luck regression changes how much of an early-inning performance the model attributes to the starter.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate trip-specific run rates by pitcher arsenal width; test breakpoint at BF 9-10.

interactions.mechanism: Tie handling and starter-change risk combine: a starter swap shifts the whole score distribution while the Tie strike pays on equal scores, so the joint PMF is a mixture over starter states with tie mass concentrated in low-total states.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute tie probability by mixture state and compare to observed tie rate by listed-starter-changed flag.

interactions.mechanism: The umpire zone matters most in low-offence environments where each walk is a bigger share of baserunners, and park/weather push toward the same margin; the interaction is a threshold in run environment where zone effects dominate pitcher's parks.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact umpire zone residual with park factor tercile in a five-inning runs model.

interactions.mechanism: The F7 result depends on how many of innings six and seven each bullpen must cover and which relievers are available: a tired bullpen after an extra-inning game forces lower-leverage arms into the sixth, and a manager leading by a run uses setup men earlier, so the same starters imply different F7 distributions by bullpen state.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare F7 scoring against F5 scoring split by bullpen pitches thrown over the previous three days and by score margin after five.

nonlinearities.shape: Step at the second and third trip boundaries in batters faced
nonlinearities.why: Run-prevention penalties apply at trip boundaries rather than smoothly, so a linear innings term misprices exit-time-weighted runs.

nonlinearities.shape: Heavily discrete with excess mass at 0 and 1 runs per team in five innings
nonlinearities.why: Low-scoring five-inning games have large tie mass; a continuous approximation misprices spread and tie strikes.

nonlinearities.shape: Convex penalty for weak starters because early exits bring in relievers
nonlinearities.why: The effective run rate for a poor starter is worse than his rate suggests because of early exits and inherited-runner effects.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating shrinkage of team-level F5 split to league mean
nonlinearities.why: Team F5-versus-bullpen splits are noisy and mostly random, so the shrink weight should be heavy and nonlinear in sample size.

contract.settlement_definition: Three live series after the reconciliation, all with sampled rules. KXMLBRFI pays Yes 'If either team scores a run in the first inning' (no secondary clause on postponement or called games). KXMLBINNINGTOTAL (both teams' combined runs in one named inning over 0.5 or over 1.5) and KXMLBINNINGWIN (one market per team 'scores more in the Nth inning' plus a tie market) count only the runs of the named inning. Kalshi's public market API (settled markets listed 2026-11-08) shows these strikes for every inning 1 through 9 of each listed game: Over 0.5 and Over 1.5 for INNINGTOTAL, team-more and tie for INNINGWIN; no extra-inning strike was listed. Every inning's text says the market resolves to a Fair Price if the game is called before that inning is completed (verified for the 3rd inning as well as the sampled 9th); only the 9th-inning text adds that it settles 'even if the home team does not bat in the bottom of the inning'. The F3/F5/F7, extras and winning-streak series formerly filed here were moved by the reconciliation. Source of truth is not named.

rules_evidence.quote: Only runs scored during the 9th inning count towards this market.
rules_evidence.establishes: Inning markets are about one inning's runs only, not cumulative score.

rules_evidence.quote: If the game is called before the 9th inning is completed this market will resolve to a Fair Price.
rules_evidence.establishes: A game called before the 9th is completed resolves the 9th-inning market at a Fair Price (a priced settlement, not a void) for the 9th-inning market.

rules_evidence.quote: the market will resolve based on runs scored in the 9th Inning even if the home team does not bat in the bottom of the inning
rules_evidence.establishes: A skipped bottom of the ninth (home lead) does not void; the inning's runs are the visitors' top-9 runs only, so the home team scores zero by construction.

rules_evidence.quote: If either team scores a run in the first inning of the Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay professional baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 28, 2026
rules_evidence.establishes: Run-in-first-inning is the union of both teams' first-half-inning events (top and bottom of the first).

rules_evidence.quote: If neither Milwaukee nor Tampa Bay scores more runs in the 9th inning
rules_evidence.establishes: The tie strike pays when the two teams' 9th-inning runs are equal, including 0-0 and the case where the home team does not bat and the visitors are held scoreless.

variants_and_edge_cases: Population differs by series: KXMLBRFI resolves on the first inning (both halves always played), while KXMLBINNINGTOTAL and KXMLBINNINGWIN resolve on the named (sampled: 9th) inning, whose bottom half may not be played or may end early on a walk-off.

Ninth-inning markets: the home team does not bat when leading, so the ninth is an at most one-half-inning event in about half of games, and the market still settles Yes/No on the visitor's runs; a game called before the 9th is completed resolves to a Fair Price.

Inning-winner construction: when the home team leads after 8.5 innings it does not bat, its 9th-inning runs are zero, so the tie strike resolves Yes exactly when the visitors are held scoreless in the top of the 9th and the home strike cannot win; when the home team bats, a non-home-run walk-off caps its 9th-inning runs at the margin needed, while a walk-off home run counts every run it scores.

KXMLBRFI has a one-sentence rule ('If either team scores a run in the first inning') with no clause for a postponed, suspended or called game, unlike the 9th-inning markets, which resolve to a Fair Price if the inning is not completed.

Inning index (verified 2026-11-08 from the Kalshi markets endpoint for KXMLBINNINGTOTAL and KXMLBINNINGWIN): innings 1-8 trade with the same two strikes as the 9th, so the archetype prices a per-inning curve across the order's 2nd and 3rd trips and the starter-to-bullpen handoff, not only the first and ninth innings; innings 1-8 always have both halves unless the game is called (Fair Price), and a walk-off can only truncate the 9th.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official linescore by inning (MLB Stats API / box score); presumed, since the sampled rules name no source.

mechanism.summary: An inning is a short Markov process over base-out states: batters come up in lineup order, each plate appearance moves the state, and the half-inning ends after three outs, giving a zero-inflated run distribution whose probability of at least one run is about a quarter to a third. For the first inning the three or four hitters due up at the top of each order face the starter's first trip, so the probability of a run in the first inning (RFI) is the union of two half-innings driven by top-of-order on-base and power skill, handedness, and the starter's first-inning command. Later-inning markets depend on which batters are due, the times-through-the-order effect and which reliever enters; the ninth inning is special because the home team may not bat and the pitcher is usually a high-leverage reliever chosen by game state. A first-principles model is a plate-appearance simulation with base-out states and pitcher-specific, count-based outcome probabilities, with strong shrinkage because inning-split samples are tiny. The cumulative F3/F5/F7, extras and winning-streak series were moved to other archetypes and are not generated here.

stages.name: Which hitters and which pitcher are in the inning
stages.description: The first inning is deterministic in who bats first: slots 1-3 of the visiting side against the starter, then 1-3 of the home side, with slot 4 and 5 appearing only if baserunners accumulate. Ninth-inning markets instead depend on the due-up slots at that point and on the pitcher chosen by score state (closer, setup, mop-up), neither known pregame. The identity and handedness of these few players is the dominant information.
stages.distribution: Deterministic for first inning, mixture over due-up slots and reliever identity for later innings.

stages.name: Half-inning base-out Markov process
stages.description: From the bases-empty, zero-out state each PA transitions among states according to the batter-pitcher outcome probabilities (walk, single, double, home run, strikeout, ball in play out); the half-inning ends at three outs. P(at least one run) is the probability of leaving the zero-run absorbing path, and expected runs per inning follow. The top three hitters' OBP and extra-base power set the entry probability and the pitcher's early command sets walks.
stages.distribution: Zero-inflated geometric-like run count per half-inning (P(0) around 0.7 to 0.75), heavier tail when runners accumulate.

stages.name: First-trip pitcher state and zone
stages.description: The starter's first trip through the order combines fresh stuff with command variance; early innings also have an umpire-zone effect and park/weather shifts, but historical first-inning splits for a single pitcher are noisy (about 30 starts per season), so inference needs heavy shrinkage toward the pitcher's PA-level skill rather than first-inning ERA.
stages.distribution: Small-sample noise dominates observed first-inning splits; true variation across pitchers is small relative to sampling error.

stages.name: Game-state conditioning for late innings
stages.description: The ninth inning depends on the score entering it: tied, one-run, save situation, blowout; the home team skips the bottom of the ninth when leading, which zeroes its 9th-inning runs and turns the inning-winner tie strike into 'visitors held scoreless'; pitcher choice follows leverage (closer in save situations, setup arms when tied, mop-up arms in blowouts). The bottom of the ninth is a stopping-rule process: the half-inning ends the moment the home team takes the lead, so the home half's runs are truncated (a walk-off home run counts all its runs; any other walk-off counts only the runs needed to take the lead), which biases a naive over-1.5 or tie estimate.
stages.distribution: State-dependent mixture over entering margin; point mass at 'bottom half not played' (home leading, roughly half of games) and a truncated home half otherwise.

stages.name: Called-game fair-price branch
stages.description: The 9th-inning markets resolve to a Fair Price if the game is called before the 9th is completed, while KXMLBRFI has no such clause and is settled once the first inning is played. A weather-shortened game is therefore a separate settlement branch for late-inning strikes: its probability depends on rain timing relative to the game's progress, and it removes the 9th-inning outcome from the payoff rather than settling it.
stages.distribution: Rare branch (a few percent of outdoor games, near zero under a roof) that grows with forecast precipitation late in the game window; zero for first-inning markets once the first inning completes.

stages.name: Middle-inning index: which trip and which arm
stages.description: Single-inning strikes for innings 2 through 8 depend on where the lineup turns over and who is pitching when that inning starts. For a given inning index the due-up slot is a random variable propagated from the earlier innings' baserunner counts, the starter's second or third trip arrives around innings 3-6 with a higher on-base rate, and the probability that a reliever opens the inning rises from near zero in the 4th to most games by the 7th. Over 1.5 rungs need two runs inside one half-inning pair, so they respond to the top-of-order turning over in that inning far more than the Over 0.5 rung.
stages.distribution: Per-inning zero-inflated run count; P(over 0.5) varies by inning index in a hump shape (higher in the 1st and around the third trip); Over 1.5 mass is concentrated in innings where slots 1-4 are due.

pace_volume.note: Batters per inning and inning-index scoring.

distribution_variance.note: Inning zero-inflation and cumulative tie mass; the season-streak extreme value is no longer claimed here.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: The inning contracts now filed here (9th inning and first inning) are single-game events whose schedule and motivation effects act only through the lineup card and bullpen availability already listed; no season-long or schedule driver changes the run probability of one half-inning.

settlement_contract.note: Per-series wording: 9th-inning counting even when the home team does not bat, Fair Price on a called game, RFI with no called-game clause.

mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.label: First-inning run probability from a base-out Markov chain with the confirmed top-4 hitters and the starter's first-trip PA outcome rates
mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.mechanism: RFI is the union of two half-innings; each is a Markov process over the first four or five hitters.
mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.rationale: First-inning ERA or RFI history is nearly pure noise; a chain built from PA-level outcome probabilities (not inning-level results) uses all the data and the confirmed order, and includes the fact that the fourth and fifth hitters bat only if the first three reach.
mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.measurement: For each half-inning: transition probabilities for batter slots 1-5 from log5-combined P(walk), P(1B), P(2B+), P(HR), P(K), P(other out) using hitter vs hand rates (shrunk to projection k = 250 PA) and starter first-time-through rates (starter first-trip PA outcomes over last 2 seasons, shrunk to league k = 300 BF). Solve the chain analytically: P(no run) = path probabilities to three outs without scoring. RFI = 1 - P(no run top) x P(no run bottom); P(top run) and P(bottom run) also output for team-specific markets. Units: probability. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: PA-level outcomes by batter and pitcher
mlb.first_inning_markov_run_prob.why: Replaces first_inning_splits as a computational estimand and removes dependence on 30-start samples.

mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.label: Ninth-inning entry state (score margin, home-bats flag) and expected pitcher and due-up slots
mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.mechanism: The 9th inning's run distribution depends on whether the home team bats, the margin, and who pitches.
mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.rationale: KXMLBINNINGTOTAL and KXMLBINNINGWIN settle on the ninth only, including the case where the home team skips the bottom. The probability that the bottom of the ninth is played falls with home-team lead probability, and the pitcher is the closer in save situations or a mop-up arm in blowouts.
mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.measurement: P(home bats bottom 9) = P(home not leading after top 9) from the run distribution after 8 innings and top-9 runs. Margin entering 9 from simulated score distribution (innings 1-8). Pitcher: P(closer) = P(save situation: lead 1-3 for the home team entering visitor's top? (visitors pitching vs home)); for the visitor's top 9 the pitcher is the home team's closer if home leads by <=3, otherwise a setup/mop-up arm. Closer availability from usage in prior 2 days (back-to-back/3-in-4 flags). Due-up slots from expected PAs through eight innings (0-8 batters). Output: expected runs in top-9 and bottom-9 and P(any run). As-of: lineup post (prior) and live updates. WALK-OFF STOPPING RULE: bottom-9 (and later) runs are computed from a half-inning chain that terminates when the home team takes the lead. Tied entering the bottom: P(any run) = P(chain reaches a go-ahead run), and the run count is 1 unless the final hit is a home run (then 1 + runners on). Home trailing by d: only the first d+1 runs can score, again with the homer exception. This truncated distribution, not the untruncated half-inning run distribution, feeds KXMLBINNINGTOTAL over 1.5 and the Tie strike of KXMLBINNINGWIN.
free_sources: MLB Stats API play-by-play (leverage, pitching changes)
raw_data: inning-level: score diff entering 9, pitcher used, inning runs, closer usage history
mlb.ninth_inning_entry_and_pitcher.why: The ninth is a state-conditional, non-exchangeable inning; no existing catalog input captures the skipped-bottom and closer selection.

mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.label: Team scoring and allowed-runs profile by inning index (1st versus 2nd-8th)
mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.mechanism: Offence is stronger early (top of order due up) and weaker late (relievers, platoon-optimised matchups).
mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.rationale: League scoring in the first inning exceeds other innings because the best hitters bat; team and park differences in first-inning versus other-inning scoring are mostly noise but have systematic pieces (starter quality, lineup top-heaviness).
mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.measurement: Per team: runs per half-inning for innings 1, 2-3, 4-6, 7-9 over last 3 seasons, shrink to league-by-inning k = 100 half-innings. Use for baseline; for team-pair adjust multiplicatively by opponent (ratio to league). Units: runs per half-inning. As-of: prior game.
raw_data: inning-level runs by team, park, home/away
mlb.inning_index_scoring_profile.why: Provides the base rate by inning index and a ceiling for how much inning-specific tendency is real.

mlb.first_inning.reason: Baseline RFI rate by park/league is a prior; observed first-inning scoring history is noisy and should not drive the model alone. Overlaps mlb.first_inning_splits (WEAK, f3_split DUPLICATE); only the park/league RFI base rate is kept, as a prior.

mlb.first_inning_splits.reason: Starter first-inning ERA splits are sample-starved (about 30 innings a year); useful only after heavy shrinkage toward PA-level skill, as the catalog itself concedes.

mlb.lineup_pit.reason: The first three or four hitters of each side decide RFI; confirmed order is the central information.

mlb.platoon.reason: Handedness of the top four against the starter matters but is part of PA-level matchup probabilities.

mlb.sp_quality.reason: Starter true talent for the first trip; separate from first-inning splits.

mlb.plate_discipline.reason: Walk and zone rates feed baserunner probability; overlaps with k_rates but distinct outcome.

mlb.k_rates.reason: Strikeouts remove baserunner chances; partially duplicated by SP quality.

mlb.f3_split.reason: Cumulative innings 1-3 run split built for KXMLBF3, which the reconciliation filed in first5_markets (now attached there); every inning market here settles on one inning's runs, so a three-inning cumulative distribution is not an input. Removed from stage s3 and the PA dataset.

mlb.tto.reason: Innings 2-8 strikes are live (verified), so the second- and third-trip penalty is what moves single-inning run probability in innings 3-7 before the starter exits; irrelevant to the first inning and replaced by the reliever in the 8th-9th.

mlb.bullpen.reason: Reliever availability determines the 9th-inning and late-inning pitcher; drives inning-level markets late.

mlb.park.reason: Run environment scales first-inning probability by a few percent.

mlb.weather_pit.reason: Weather has small effects at inning level and is mostly captured in park norms.

mlb.umpire.reason: Zone effects early; modest for one inning.

mlb.run_dist.reason: Needed for cumulative tie mass and ninth-inning entry state; per-inning distribution required.

m.rules_text.reason: Series differ (Fair Price on called games for the 9th-inning markets, none for RFI; 9th inning counted even if the home team does not bat), so wording per series decides the object.

mlb.babip_luck.reason: BABIP regression at inning scale is meaningless; relevant only to the rate estimates feeding the Markov chain. Removed from stage s2 inputs by resolver; no inning-scale use remains.

interactions.mechanism: A run in the first inning requires baserunners from the top three and then enough extra-base power or walks to convert, so the probability depends on the product of leadoff on-base skill, the number-three hitter's power and the pitcher's walk rate rather than their sum. A lineup top with two high-OBP hitters against a command-poor starter compounds.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare RFI log loss from the chain (product) versus additive top-three wOBA models.

interactions.mechanism: The ninth-inning run distribution has three regimes: save situation with closer (low run probability), tied or one-run with high-leverage arms, and blowout with mop-up arms; home-bats flag changes whether the bottom exists. The regime probabilities come from the score distribution, so ninth-inning markets are a mixture priced by margin.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate P(run in top-9) by entry margin bucket and closer availability; compare with unconditional average.

interactions.mechanism: Whether the ninth is played at all, and how many runs it can contain, depends on the margin entering the bottom half: a home lead removes it, a tie or one-run deficit ends it at the go-ahead run, and the due-up hitters set how often that run arrives. The truncation lowers over-1.5 and Tie-strike probabilities relative to the untruncated half-inning run distribution, most for tied games with a high-OBP due-up group.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare observed bottom-9 run distributions for tied-entering and trailing-entering games against the untruncated Markov chain output, split by due-up OBP tercile.

interactions.mechanism: Platoon advantage of the top of the order is conditional on the starter's pitch arsenal: a lefty-heavy top against a right-hander with a good changeup differs from the same top against a slider-only right-hander; the effect is realised in the first trip where hitters have not adjusted.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact top-four handedness share with starter changeup/slider usage in a first-trip PA model.

interactions.mechanism: The KXMLBINNINGWIN tie strike is a joint event of top- and bottom-9th runs: when the home team leads it equals P(visitors score 0 against the home closer or setup man); when tied or trailing the home half is truncated at the winning run, so a 1-1 or 2-2 ninth is rarer than independent half-innings imply and 0-0 dominates. The weight on each case comes from the margin distribution entering the ninth and from which relievers are available.
interactions.how_to_test: Tabulate historical 9th-inning run pairs by entering margin and compare tie frequency with a model that treats the two halves as independent untruncated innings.

interactions.mechanism: For innings 3-6 the run probability of a named inning switches regime on whether the starter is still in: while he pitches, the third-trip penalty raises it; once a fresh reliever opens the inning it falls back toward the bullpen's rate, so the inning-index curve is a mixture weighted by the starter's survival to that inning.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare actual runs in innings 4-7 split by starter-in versus reliever-opened against the inning-index profile alone; a significant split coefficient at fixed inning index shows the regime.

nonlinearities.shape: Zero-inflated, convex: P(run) rises convexly with top-three OBP because the chain compounds across hitters
nonlinearities.why: Extra baserunners make each later batter more valuable (runner-on states), so the probability of at least one run grows faster than linearly in on-base skill.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating weight with innings pitched: weight on pitcher-specific first-inning history rises slowly and stays low
nonlinearities.why: First-inning outcomes are rare events with heavy sampling noise; the shrinkage weight should grow roughly with the number of innings but remain small.

nonlinearities.shape: Discrete mass at 0 runs per inning (about 72%) with geometric tail
nonlinearities.why: Inning scores are zero-inflated so a normal approximation fails for 0.5 and 1.5 strikes.

nonlinearities.shape: Step by margin entering the ninth: save situation (lead 1-3) versus blowout
nonlinearities.why: Pitcher quality and run probability change discontinuously around the save-situation boundary.

nonlinearities.shape: Absorbing truncation: the bottom-9 run count is capped at the margin needed to take the lead (plus homer exception)
nonlinearities.why: The home half ends on the go-ahead run, so P(2+ runs in the bottom 9) is far below the untruncated chain value in tied or one-run games; this is a stopping-rule nonlinearity distinct from the save-situation step.

contract.settlement_definition: Two live series with sampled rules, now filed here. KXMLBEXTRAS: Yes 'If at least 1 extra inning is played' in the named game, i.e. the score is level after nine complete innings (no secondary rules text). KXMLBDELAY: Yes if the game originally scheduled for the date 'is officially delayed due to weather', which 'includes a delayed start time as well as any suspension or stoppage of play after the event has begun due to weather'; delays caused solely by other reasons resolve No. Neither text addresses a game postponed before first pitch, a suspended game resumed later, or names a data source.

rules_evidence.quote: If at least 1 extra inning is played in the Milwaukee vs Tampa Bay professional baseball game originally scheduled for Oct 28, 2026
rules_evidence.establishes: The extras market is a regulation-tie event: any tenth inning settles Yes.

rules_evidence.quote: This includes a delayed start time as well as any suspension or stoppage of play after the event has begun due to weather.
rules_evidence.establishes: Both start delays and in-game weather stoppages count, regardless of length.

rules_evidence.quote: Delays caused solely by reasons other than weather do not count and will result in a No resolution.
rules_evidence.establishes: Non-weather delays (lighting failure, crowd) resolve No.

variants_and_edge_cases: The two contract families are unrelated mechanically: extras is a function of the run distribution (a regulation tie), delay is a weather-timing event unrelated to team quality, and a shared model would conflate them.

Delay definition counts both a delayed start time and any in-game weather stoppage regardless of duration, so even short (five-minute) stoppages count if recorded as official delays; a postponed game (no first pitch that day) is not described.

Extras requires the game to remain tied after the top and bottom of the ninth (the bottom is played only if the home team does not lead); a game called by weather while tied before the ninth is a suspension or shortened game, not extras.
A suspended game completed later with extra innings is attached to 'originally scheduled' date in the sampled wording but handling is unstated.
contract.settlement_data_source: Official linescore (innings played) for extras; official game log/box-score delay record for weather delays (MLB Stats API, box score 'delay' line); presumed, since neither sampled text names a source.

mechanism.summary: Two event families share the archetype and are mechanically unrelated. Extra innings occur when the two teams' nine-inning run totals are equal, so the probability is the tie mass of the difference of two overdispersed run counts, adjusted by the structure that the home team skips the bottom ninth when ahead; it is highest in low-scoring, evenly matched games and is a few percentage points higher than naive Poisson-based estimates because runs correlate positively across teams through park and weather. Delay markets are weather-timing problems: a delay requires precipitation, lightning within the league's safety radius, or severe wind/temperature conditions overlapping the game window while the roof is open or absent, and the umpire crew and team officials decide to stop or hold play. The probability depends on forecast timing and convective structure rather than team quality, and on how the contract defines delay (start versus in-game, any duration). Both are low-to-moderate probability events where the contract's exact wording and the quality of timing information decide edge.

stages.name: Regulation score distribution and tie mass
stages.description: Extras occur only if the score is level after nine complete innings. The tie mass is the sum over k of P(away = k) P(home = k) with a positive dependence between teams, so a low expected total and a close pairing raise it. The home team's skipped bottom of the ninth does not create extras; it removes them in games where the home team leads.
stages.distribution: Tie probability about 8-10% of games; sensitive to total: low-total games tie more; positive team-run correlation raises tie mass.

stages.name: Late-inning resolution before extras
stages.description: Extras happen when the score is level after nine complete innings. The main routes are a tie after the top of the 9th that the home team fails to break, and a one-or-more-run visitor lead that the home team equalises without taking the lead; a home lead after 8.5 innings removes the bottom half entirely. The bottom-9 half-inning is a stopping-rule process: it ends the moment the home team takes the lead, so run totals are truncated and the P(level) depends on the closer, the due-up hitters and the deficit entering the half.
stages.distribution: Conditional probability of the home team scoring at least once in a tied bottom 9 is roughly 27-32% for a typical reliever (league P(run) per half-inning is about 0.27); lower against elite closers. The extras event is Bernoulli with a mixture over the entering run differential.

stages.name: Weather exposure over the game window
stages.description: Delay requires weather in the window: precipitation timing relative to first pitch and the expected 3-hour game, lightning within eight miles (league and stadium safety rules), heavy wind or cold in some venues, and a roof that is open, closed, or retractable with a decision made before first pitch. The same forecast yields different delay probabilities across parks with and without roofs and with different drainage.
stages.distribution: Binary event with probability about 5-10% overall, near 0 in domes and up to 30-50% on convectively active evenings.

stages.name: Decision and recording process
stages.description: Whether weather becomes an official delay depends on umpire and home-team judgement and on the way the delay is recorded: a start delayed by tarp, an in-game stoppage, a rain-shortened or suspended game, or a postponement. Short delays may not be recorded in the structured data, and a postponed game is not a delayed one under the sampled wording.
stages.distribution: Threshold decision with human judgement; recording rules produce a minimum recorded duration in data.

stages.name: Interaction between the two events
stages.description: Extras lengthen the game and thereby increase exposure to in-game weather delays, so a delay contract that counts in-game stoppages is mildly positively related to extras; start-delay contracts are unaffected. For the extras contract, a suspended game (weather) tied in the middle is not extras.
stages.distribution: Small positive dependence through game length; negligible for start delays.

talent_strength.note: Run-prevention quality drives total and tie mass.

efficiency_conversion.note: Conversion of the home half-inning into a walk-off run.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Game length exposure for in-game delays.

role_personnel.note: Neither event depends on which individual players start beyond what the run distribution already captures; delays depend on weather and officials rather than roster composition, and extras on aggregate scoring, so no separate personnel driver is needed.

availability_news.note: Confirmed starters and scratches enter through sp_quality (as-of lineup post), the roof open/closed decision through roof_state, and postponement/forecast updates through forecast_precip_timing; lineup-card vintage is tracked as an open item (ext_lineup_vintage).

pace_volume.note: Pace of play affects when the bottom of the ninth is reached and game duration, but not the tie probability or delay occurrence in a way sampled contracts can price, so no pace driver is added.

mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.label: Tie probability after nine innings from joint (correlated) run distributions
mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.mechanism: The tie mass depends on the correlation of the two teams' runs through park and weather and on the discrete shapes.
mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.rationale: Independent-NB convolution underestimates ties because shared park/weather effects make both teams' totals move together; high-scoring environments widen the distribution and lower tie mass per run level.
mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.measurement: Compute P(tie after 9) = sum_k P(R_a=k, R_h=k) from a bivariate NB or copula with correlation rho_park calibrated on 10 seasons of games by park (shrink k = 300 games) and by wind-out indicator; adjust for home team skipping bottom 9 (P(home leads after 8.5) removes some games). Calibrate against observed extras rate by expected-total decile. Units: probability. As-of: lineup post.
raw_data: game-level runs by team, innings played, park, wind, temperature
mlb.team_run_correlation_tie_mass.why: KXMLBEXTRAS settles on the tie event, so the joint distribution (not each team's total) is the right object.

mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.label: P(extra innings) from the inning-by-inning score chain, including tie-restoring bottom-9 halves
mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.mechanism: Extras occur whenever the score is level after nine complete innings (or after the home half is played to its end), so the event is a function of the joint inning-by-inning chain, not of a single tied-entering-the-ninth conditional.
mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.rationale: KXMLBEXTRAS pays when at least one extra inning is played. Games reach extras by two routes: tied after the top of the 9th with the home team failing to score, and visitors leading after the top of the 9th with the home team tying the score but not taking the lead (the half-inning ends on the third out, not on the tying run). Modelling only the first route understates P(extras); the home walk-off stopping rule also truncates the bottom-9 run distribution.
mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.measurement: P(extras) = sum over states s of P(state s entering bottom 9) x P(home half-inning ends with score level), computed from an inning-by-inning Markov chain: states are (run differential after top 9, outs=0) with visitor closer PA rates (shrunk to league reliever rates, k = 150 BF) and home due-up hitters. Tied entering bottom 9: P(level) = P(home scores 0). Home trailing by d>=1: P(level) = P(home scores exactly d runs without taking the lead, the half ends on the third out). Home leading: no bottom 9, P(extras)=0. Walk-off stopping rule applied, so the half-inning ends once the home team takes the lead. Validate on 5 seasons by comparing predicted and observed extras rate by pre-game expected-total decile. Units: probability. As-of: confirmed lineups.
raw_data: half-inning-level: tied entering bottom 9 flag, pitcher, due-up slots, runs scored
mlb.tie_entering_ninth_resolution.why: Defines P(extras) as P(level score after nine complete innings) so both extras routes are included.

mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.label: Lightning-proximity exposure within the league's 8-mile safety radius over the game window
mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.mechanism: Lightning within a set radius triggers mandatory delays independent of rain amount.
mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.rationale: A forecast of rain probability misses thunderstorms with sparse precipitation; lightning radius rules cause delays even when the field is dry, and conversely rain can come without lightning and be played through.
mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.measurement: Target: P(at least one lightning flash within 8 miles of the park from first pitch to first pitch + 3.5 hours). Historical frequency f(park, month, local hour) from GOES-R GLM flashes (2018 onward) within 8 miles of park coordinates. Forecast-conditioned probability from a logistic regression of the flash indicator on forecast CAPE and probability of thunder at the vintage 3 hours before first pitch, calibrated on 5 seasons of games and shrunk to f with k = 40 games per park-month. Separately calibrate P(delay | flash) against recorded weather delays. The 8-mile radius is a modelling convention, not a league rule; GLM optical flashes proxy NLDN strikes. As-of: 3 hours before first pitch and lineup post.
raw_data: strike or flash timestamp and coordinates
mlb.lightning_proximity_exposure.why: Distinguishes lightning-driven from rain-driven delays and sharpens the weather gate.

mlb.official_delay_record_definition.label: Minimum recorded delay duration and recording rule in official game data
mlb.official_delay_record_definition.mechanism: The contract counts any official weather delay; whether short stoppages are recorded determines what the data can verify.
mlb.official_delay_record_definition.rationale: If delays under about ten minutes are not recorded in the box score or play-by-play, history underestimates the event, and the question of whether a five-minute tarp pause counts is a contract question.
mlb.official_delay_record_definition.measurement: From 5 seasons of game-feed data: (a) recorded delays = games with a Delay event or box-score 'Game delayed' note, duration = end-start; (b) detected stoppages = gaps between consecutive pitch endTime and next startTime greater than 10 minutes within an inning (excluding inning breaks, pitching changes, challenges); (c) recording rate by duration bucket (<10, 10-30, 30-60, >60 minutes) = recorded / detected, with Beta(1,1) smoothing; (d) P(recorded | hourly precipitation > 0.1 inch during game window) by bucket. Output the share of games with a recorded delay by bucket and the unrecorded share of detected gaps. Units: probability. As-of: seasons completed before the as-of date.
raw_data: game feed playEvents startTime/endTime per pitch
game feed delay events and box-score notes (reason, duration)
mlb.official_delay_record_definition.why: Defines the empirical event frequency and tests the sensitivity of the market to the recording threshold.

mlb.extras_prob.reason: A historical tie-after-nine base rate by total/spread bucket is a calibration target and prior; the generator is the run distribution.

mlb.run_dist.reason: Tie mass is its direct output; needs joint (correlated) form not marginals.

mlb.sp_quality.reason: Starter quality moves the expected total and thereby tie mass; second-order for a regulation tie.

mlb.bullpen_talent.reason: Late-inning scoring and closer quality affect tied-game resolution.

mlb.park.reason: Run environment shifts tie mass; extreme parks matter.

mlb.ghost_runner_strategy.reason: Ghost-runner strategy applies after extras begin; it does not change whether extras occur, which is what both contracts settle on.

mlb.delay_risk.reason: Described as precipitation probability, radar and roof state, which are exactly forecast_precip_timing and roof_state; the base-rate part is a calibration target.

mlb.forecast_precip_timing.reason: Timing of rain relative to first pitch and the game window is the main driver of weather delay.

mlb.roof_state.reason: A closed roof removes delay exposure; retractable-roof decision timing is crucial.

mlb.weather_pit.reason: Lightning, wind and temperature extremes; superset of the other weather inputs, so overlap.

mlb.game_completion_rules.reason: Official game thresholds and suspended-game rules determine what 'delayed' and 'extras' mean in odd cases.

m.rules_text.reason: Delay definition (start vs in-game) and extras scope define the event; versions must be tracked.

m.lifecycle.reason: Market close time versus first pitch determines which weather information is available but is not an input to the event.

interactions.mechanism: Extras probability is the diagonal of the joint score distribution; shared park and weather push both teams' runs the same way, increasing diagonal mass at any given total. The effect is largest in extreme parks where the common factor is largest.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit bivariate NB with park-specific correlation and compare tie frequency by park to independent convolution.

interactions.mechanism: Delay probability is the product of weather overlapping the window and the roof being open; for retractable roofs the decision to close depends on forecast confidence, so closed-roof parks have near-zero delay, and the gating is a regime switch. Lightning adds delays on dry fields.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate P(delay) with roof-type interaction and lightning indicator; compare calibration by roof type.

interactions.mechanism: Extras equal tie after top 9 times failure to walk off; the failure probability depends on closer quality, so for elite closers the extras probability is lower for the same tie probability.
interactions.how_to_test: Decompose extras frequency into tie and non-walk-off components and test closer effect.

interactions.mechanism: KXMLBDELAY's text counts in-game weather stoppages as well as a delayed start, so extra innings add weather exposure only while no start delay has been recorded; once any start delay occurs the market is already Yes and game length no longer matters. The dependence on extras is therefore conditional on the pre-game weather state.
interactions.how_to_test: Condition delay frequency on extras flag in historical data and compare with start-only delay frequency.

interactions.mechanism: Recorded delays follow a threshold in precipitation intensity and duration; light drizzle is played through while heavy rain triggers a tarp, so the response of delay probability to rain probability is steeply nonlinear above a threshold.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit logistic of recorded delay on forecast precipitation intensity and duration; test breakpoint.

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold/saturating: delay probability low below about 30% precipitation chance, steep between 40-70%, saturating near 90%
nonlinearities.why: Delay requires rain or lightning to actually occur during play and be heavy enough, so the response to forecast probability is S-shaped.

nonlinearities.shape: Tie mass peaks at low totals: P(tie) falls convexly as expected total rises
nonlinearities.why: The diagonal of the joint distribution thins as variance grows, so tie probability is decreasing and convex in expected total.

nonlinearities.shape: Binary gate: closed roof reduces delay probability to near zero regardless of forecast
nonlinearities.why: The roof removes exposure, so weather inputs matter only when open.

nonlinearities.shape: Approximate threshold (assumed convention): a strike within about 8 miles commonly triggers a roughly 30-minute hold, independent of strike count
nonlinearities.why: League safety protocol makes delay a step function of lightning proximity rather than intensity. This is an assumed convention, not a published uniform MLB rule; the threshold distance and hold length vary by stadium and umpire crew.

contract.settlement_definition: No MLB announcer-mention series appears in the series ledger and no rules text was sampled, so the settlement object cannot be stated from evidence: for a word-mention market the YES condition would be that a named word or phrase is spoken in a specified broadcast, but which feed (national, home, away, radio, Spanish-language), which speakers, whether pre/post-game segments count, whether on-screen graphics or sponsor reads count, how plural or inflected forms count, and what happens in a delay, postponement or extra innings are all unknown.
variants_and_edge_cases: Feed ambiguity: a national telecast, a regional sports network home feed and an away feed have different crews and vocabularies; the contract's named source decides which crew's language rate applies.
Counting rules (exact word versus stem, spoken versus on-screen, ad reads, replay clips, pre- and post-game shows) change the effective exposure by large factors and are unknown for MLB.
Broadcast length varies with game duration, extra innings and delays, so exposure time is itself random, and a postponed or suspended game restarts the clock.
Event-triggered words (player milestones, injuries, umpire controversies) have near-zero base rate that jumps if the trigger occurs; the market is a mixture over trigger realisation.
contract.settlement_data_source: Unknown: presumably a transcript or video review by Kalshi's resolver of the named broadcast; no MLB series or rule text sampled to confirm.

mechanism.summary: A word-mention market is a count of spoken occurrences in an exposure window, settled Yes if the count is at least one. The generating process is a point process: each crew has a baseline per-hour rate for each word, shaped by its vocabulary and by the broadcast format (national versus local, play-by-play versus color), multiplied by the length of the broadcast (nine innings take about two and a half to three hours, extras and delays extend it), plus event-triggered bursts when game events make the word relevant (a no-hitter in progress, a milestone, weather, injuries, the name of a player who comes to bat). Baseball statistics offer weak direct signal; most of the information is which crew is on the air, what the game script will produce, and who the players of interest are. Occurrences cluster because topics persist, so counts are overdispersed and the probability of at least one is lower than the Poisson at the same mean for low-rate words and higher for topic-driven words. Little structured data exists, so the quality of any prior depends on building transcripts.

stages.name: Which broadcast and crew
stages.description: The contract names a broadcast; its crew (play-by-play announcer, color analyst, sideline reporter), network (national such as Fox, ESPN, TBS, or the local regional network) and language determine the vocabulary and the style. National postseason crews differ from local crews in word choice, in discussion of rivalry and in sponsor language. The same game can have different feeds with very different base rates.
stages.distribution: Categorical crew identity with heterogeneous base-rate distributions; crew changes (injury or schedule) rare but discrete.

stages.name: Exposure time
stages.description: The window is the broadcast, which runs from first pitch to the final out plus any specified pre- and post-game segments; time depends on pace of play, pitching changes, extras and weather delays. Exposure is random: a seven-inning game or a delayed game changes the available time by tens of minutes, and a game called early shortens it.
stages.distribution: Right-skewed duration (about 2.4 to 3.2 hours typical; delays add up to hours); extras add about 15-20 minutes per inning.

stages.name: Word base rate per crew
stages.description: Given exposure, the count of a specific word follows a point process with a crew-specific rate per hour; common baseball words are near-certain to occur, while rare or topical words have rates below one per game. Rates differ by crew because of verbal habits (frequent use of 'Statcast', specific player nicknames, sponsor read phrases).
stages.distribution: Poisson-like with overdispersion; zero-inflated for rare words; per-crew rate heterogeneity.

stages.name: Triggered topics and named entities
stages.description: Words referring to events or people occur only when the game or the news makes them relevant: a pitcher's perfect game attempt, a milestone, a player returning from injury, a trade, weather, an umpire dispute, a rivalry. Names of players are used in proportion to their involvement (plate appearances, pitching) and storylines. These are bursts above the base rate with probabilities that depend on game events and pregame narratives.
stages.distribution: Event-triggered bursts: probability of word given trigger is high, trigger probability low; mixture structure.

stages.name: Counting rules and clustering
stages.description: What counts (inflections, spoken versus displayed, ads) changes the effective exposure and rate; counts cluster because once a topic is introduced it is repeated, so the distribution is overdispersed and the probability of at least one relative to the mean is shape-dependent. The settlement resolver's counting also introduces measurement noise.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed (negative-binomial or self-exciting) count; P(count >= 1) depends on dispersion parameter and zero mass.

settlement_contract.note: No MLB mention series exists in the ledger and no rules text was sampled, so which feed, speakers, segments, ad reads and inflections count is unknown; m.rules_text and sponsor_read_inventory cannot be claimed as coverage until a contract exists.

opponent_matchup.note: The opposing team's identity matters only through named-entity words (players on the field) and storylines, which are carried by player involvement and narrative triggers; baseball matchup quality is not a driver of what announcers say beyond that, so no separate matchup variable is defined.

officiating_rules.note: Umpire and rules affect word counts only when a controversy arises, which is already a narrative trigger rather than a regular officiating factor; no regular officiating variable changes the rate of ordinary words.

mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.label: Crew-specific word and phrase rate per broadcast hour with dispersion (transcript-based)
mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.mechanism: Each crew has a characteristic per-hour rate for each lexeme and a dispersion beyond Poisson.
mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.rationale: The catalog's mention_text names crew language tendencies without a measurement; the question needs per-word per-crew rates and a dispersion estimate because probability of at least one is concave in the rate and depends on clustering.
mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.measurement: From transcripts (ASR with timestamps) of 40+ games per crew: for each word w count n_gw and exposure hours t_g; fit negative-binomial n_gw ~ NB(mean = t_g * lambda_cw, dispersion phi_cw) with lambda_cw shrunk to national lexeme rate with k = 6 games and phi pooled by word class. Stemming rules follow the contract text version. P(at least one) = 1 - integrated NB zero probability given expected exposure. As-of: before first pitch with crew known.
free_sources: Own ASR transcripts of broadcast audio
Closed captions from MLB.TV or broadcast (SOURCE_UNVERIFIED)
raw_data: game-crew-word counts with timestamps and exposure hours
mlb.word_rate_per_broadcast_hour.why: The market is a Poisson-like exposure market with crew-specific rates; without these the probability is unanchored.

mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.label: Broadcast airtime distribution (game duration with delay and extras scenarios, plus included pre/post segments)
mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.mechanism: Exposure is the time on air, a random variable depending on pace, extras, delays and scheduling.
mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.rationale: The mention count scales with airtime, but airtime is uncertain: from a pitch-clock game of 2h25m to a 4h delayed extra-inning game, and pre/post segments may be inside or outside the contract window.
mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.measurement: Simulate duration = base minutes (team pair mean time per game, 2023+ pitch-clock regime, half-life 60 games) + 17 minutes x extra innings + delay minutes with probability from delay_risk; shift for pre-game and post-game windows if counted. Output distribution of exposure hours. Shrink team-pair means to league with k = 25 games. As-of: lineup post. Units: hours.
raw_data: game-level duration, innings, delays, start time
mlb.broadcast_airtime_distribution.why: Converts a per-hour word rate into a per-game probability.

mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.label: Player and team name mention rate as a function of involvement (PA, pitching, storyline salience)
mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.mechanism: Names are said when players are in the action or in the news, in proportion to involvement.
mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.rationale: A market on a specific player's name depends on whether he plays, bats in high-leverage spots, pitches, is injured or traded; base-rate tables for common baseball words do not apply.
mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.measurement: Model: mentions of player p per game = a_p x (PA_p + BF_p) + b_p x storyline_flag(p) with a_p estimated from 30+ transcribed games shrunk to role-class (star, regular, bench, pitcher) k = 10 games; storyline_flag from news on the previous 3 days (injury return, milestone, award talk). Zero when the player is not active. Units: mentions per game. As-of: lineup post.
mlb.player_involvement_mention_rate.why: Name-based markets are driven by involvement, not by baseball skill statistics.

mlb.sponsor_read_inventory.label: Scripted sponsor/promo read inventory and tagline language by network
mlb.sponsor_read_inventory.mechanism: Sponsor reads and promos are repeated at fixed cadence and contain fixed vocabulary.
mlb.sponsor_read_inventory.rationale: Words from sponsor segments have near-deterministic rates if the contract counts them; unknown whether they count, but they inflate the rates for brand names and phrases.
mlb.sponsor_read_inventory.measurement: From transcripts: segments classified as sponsor read via keyword templates (for example 'presented by', 'brought to you by'); per-network reads per half-hour and vocabulary, scheduled by network and time. Rate of word w in reads = reads per hour x P(w in read text). Units: occurrences per hour. As-of: network schedule for the date.
mlb.sponsor_read_inventory.why: CONDITIONAL on contract text: only relevant if a future contract counts ad reads or sponsor segments; otherwise exclude it. Separates the deterministic scripted part of language from spontaneous commentary and respects counting rules.

mlb.mention_text.reason: The core base-rate information, but as defined has no measurement or data source; word_rate_per_broadcast_hour provides the estimand.

mlb.broadcast_crew.reason: Crew and network identity set the base rate; the feed named by the contract must match.

mlb.game_narrative_triggers.reason: Event-triggered bursts for topical words; unknowable pregame except for scheduled milestones and weather.

mlb.news.reason: Storylines announcers will discuss; helps name and topic words; only useful for named entities.

mlb.delay_risk.reason: Adds airtime when delays occur; effect small on word probability except for rare words.

mlb.extras_prob.reason: Extra airtime from extras is modest (about 15-20 minutes per inning); second-order versus crew.

mlb.series_context.reason: Postseason series state changes language and national crews; present only in the playoffs.

m.rules_text.reason: Counting rules and feed definition are the entire object; absent for MLB, so it is a blocking gap.

m.quote_history.reason: Prices are market-implied probabilities, not information about announcer vocabulary.

m.strike_hit_rates.reason: Historical realised frequency by word type is a base rate for calibration, not a driver; tiny samples for MLB.

interactions.mechanism: P(at least one mention) = 1 - exp(-rate x hours) saturates in exposure for common words but is nearly linear for rare ones, so extending airtime by extras or delays matters only for words whose rate times hours is below about two. Crew determines the rate that sets which regime applies.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit P(word) as function of crew-specific rate and airtime; compare to linear approximation for rare and common words.

interactions.mechanism: Topical words occur at baseline until a trigger fires, after which the rate jumps; the market probability is the mixture P(trigger) x P(word|trigger) + (1-P(trigger)) x baseline. Scheduled triggers (milestone chase, rivalry games) are visible pregame, but in-game triggers (no-hitter, injury) are not.
interactions.how_to_test: Condition word frequency on trigger flags in transcripts and test mixture versus homogeneous rate.

interactions.mechanism: National versus local feed and counting rules (sponsors, graphics) switch the effective vocabulary; a contract limited to the national feed uses a different crew and sponsor mix than the home feed, so probability is determined first by the regime then by the rate. This holds only if a contract that counts ad reads exists (none in the ledger); treat as conditional.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate word rates separately by feed type and counting rule version; compare out-of-sample calibration.

interactions.mechanism: A player's name rate multiplies his involvement (PA, pitching) and the storyline salience (return from injury, award talk); a star in a storyline gets a rate several times a bench player's, and a non-starter gets zero, so involvement gates the storyline effect.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit mention-rate model with involvement x storyline interaction on transcripts.

interactions.mechanism: Delays and extras both lengthen the broadcast but are nearly independent events with different tails; the airtime distribution is a convolution with a heavy right tail, so rare-word probabilities have a fat contribution from long-game scenarios.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate airtime from separate delay and extras processes and check the correlation with game duration data.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating: P(word) = 1 - E[(1+lambda*t/phi)^(-phi)] (negative-binomial zero probability), not the Poisson 1-exp(-lambda*t)
nonlinearities.why: Each additional minute adds less once the word has a high chance of already having occurred. Dispersion-adjusted: clustering of topical words means the Poisson form overstates P(at least one) for the same mean rate; phi is estimated per word class.

nonlinearities.shape: Overdispersion with zero inflation: P(0) far above Poisson for topical words
nonlinearities.why: Clustering and topic persistence make many games have none and a few have many, which changes P(at least one).

nonlinearities.shape: Threshold: probability jumps once the trigger occurs (no-hitter after the 6th inning, milestone in sight)
nonlinearities.why: Topical language is gated by event occurrence, producing a step in rate.

nonlinearities.shape: Linear in PA but jump in high-leverage PA or milestones
nonlinearities.why: Name frequency scales with action, with additional jumps in salient moments.
